title: qa-gate.sh reports status=recorded when bd resolves a different workspace: for design-record the comment IS the deliverable
description:
Found by the devops specialist while testing the D1 R1/R2 fix round, 2026-08-12. Pre-existing and
generic to qa-gate.sh; deliberately NOT folded into D1.

MECHANISM. bd resolves its database from the CURRENT WORKING DIRECTORY. require_bd only checks that
$PROJECT_DIR/.beads exists - not that bd will actually resolve THAT workspace from where the script
is being run. add_comment is best-effort. So a subcommand invoked from a cwd outside the Beads
workspace reports status=recorded on stdout while the comment never lands anywhere.

WHY IT IS WORSE FOR design-record THAN FOR THE OTHERS. For most subcommands the comment is a durable
side-record of an action whose primary effect is elsewhere (a label, an exit code, a file). For
design-record THE COMMENT IS THE DELIVERABLE: the DESIGN-ARTIFACT record carrying design_hash is the
entire output, and every downstream reader - approve's binding check, the D2 review loop, D6's
coherence rollup - reads that comment. A silent no-op here is indistinguishable from success and
leaves the design phase with no binding at all, while the caller is told it succeeded.

THE SHAPE IS THE RELEASE'S OWN DEFECT CLASS: a claim (status=recorded) that outran its mechanism
(a best-effort write to a database that may not be the one anybody reads).

NEEDS: either resolve bd against PROJECT_DIR explicitly rather than inheriting the cwd, or verify the
comment landed and fail loudly when it did not. Prefer verification - the repo already established
this idiom in remove_label, which runs the removal then re-reads and returns non-zero if the label
survived, precisely because 'without this every rollback block above is decorative'. Pair with a leg
that runs the subcommand from a foreign cwd and asserts a non-zero exit, plus a control proving the
ordinary in-workspace path still succeeds.

title: D0 deviation: orchestrator and reviewer ship `top`, not the plan's Opus-class — land the plan's tiers in D4
description:
Recorded deviation from the v5 plan's Phase D0 role mapping (QA finding R1-F3 on claude-workflow-plugin-fkm.2).

THE PLAN (docs/plans/v5-design-phase.md:86-92) specifies five rows. D0 ships three of them
as specified-or-corrected and two of them differently:

| role | plan | shipped in D0 | covered by a correction? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| designer | latest Fable-class | `top` | YES — correction 7 |
| design_reviewer | OpenAI reasoning, fallback Fable-class | `top` + design_reviewer_lane | YES — correction 7 |
| implementer | latest Sonnet-class | `sonnet-class` | n/a — as specified |
| orchestrator | latest Opus-class | `top` (Fable today) | NO |
| reviewer | Sol via Codex, fallback latest Opus-class | `top` + reviewer_lane (Sol half IS implemented) | NO |

WHY CORRECTION 7 DOES NOT COVER THESE TWO. Correction 7 says a family-pinned strategy kills
day-zero adoption of a new top family and that `top` "expresses the same intent". That holds

- D0 already lands one tier drop (implementer opus-class -> sonnet-class) ahead of the machinery
  meant to absorb it. A second drop in the same phase compounds that sequencing risk.
- `reviewer` is the gate's own seat; dropping review capability while the design phases are
  being built is the wrong direction for the surface that catches everything else.

WHEN: D4 (claude-workflow-plugin-fkm.6), where the plan itself narrows the orchestrator's job to
execution planning and the design lanes carry the design work.

THE CHANGE: two lines in .claude/model-roles (`orchestrator=opus-class`, `reviewer=opus-class`),
plus re-checking the identity-collapse condition (with reviewer on opus-class and the design
lanes on top, nothing collapses) and the statusline group render (four groups, so the ` +<k>
more` tail arms — .claude/scripts/tests/model-roles.test.sh section 4 covers that shape).

If the orchestrator reads the plan's table as a D7 END-STATE rather than a D0 deliverable, this
task is the place to record that reading and close it.

Either .claude/model-roles carries the plan's tiers for orchestrator and reviewer, or this task
records the decision that `top` is the intended end state for both, with the reason. Whichever
way it goes, the .claude/model-roles header rider and the CHANGELOG note added in fkm.2 R1 are
updated to match, so the file and the release notes never disagree about what shipped.

title: specs/model-select.sh writes fixed /tmp/ms-*.err paths: two concurrent component runs clobber each other
description:
Found by qa-claude during the D0 review, 2026-08-12.

.claude/tests/component/specs/model-select.sh writes FIXED paths under /tmp (ms-*.err), so two
concurrent L2 runs on one host overwrite each other's error capture. The only interlock anywhere
in the tree is the orchestrator's own pgrep busy-guard, which guards ONE side: it stops a second
run the orchestrator starts, and does nothing about a run started by a reviewer, a specialist, or
a human.

OBSERVED IN THIS SESSION, twice, on unrelated grounds:
- qa-claude's pristine-HEAD baseline overlapped the orchestrator's confirming bar's component
  tier ~09:07-09:26 on 2026-08-12. QA killed its own run and reaped the orphaned per-spec
  children, and explicitly left a measurement UNVERIFIED rather than report a number taken
  under contention.
- Earlier the same day, verify-before-stop.sh launched a second make test 53s after the
  orchestrator's pgrep guard had already fired, so two L1 suites ran for ~26 minutes.

WHY IT MATTERS BEFORE D4. Phase D4 computes PARALLEL BATCHES and D5 runs them in worktrees. The
moment more than one batch runs a component tier, fixed /tmp paths are a cross-run data race whose
failure mode is a wrong error message attached to the right spec - i.e. a misleading diagnosis,
which is this release's whole subject.

NEEDS: per-run scratch (mktemp -d under the runner's RUN_SCRATCH, which now exists), plus a leg
that reds if a fixed /tmp path is reintroduced - a grep census over the spec directory, paired
with a control proving the census can fail. Note LESSONS on per-run tokens: the same class already
bit runner-completeness.test.sh via machine-global pgrep literals.

title: bd 1.2.1 re-accepts `bd sync` — bd-compat.sh pinned range and README 'Supported bd range' need updating
description:
Found while measuring Phase D0 (claude-workflow-plugin-fkm.2). NOT caused by that change set — `bd-compat.sh` is unmodified by D0 and nothing in D0 mentions `bd sync`.

WHAT MOVED: the `bd` binary on this machine went 1.1.2 -> 1.2.1 mid-session.
  `bd --version` => `bd version 1.2.1 (634cbbc4b)`

SYMPTOM: one assertion in the L2 component spec `.claude/tests/component/specs/bd-compat.sh` goes red:

  FAIL: bd-compat[sync (REMOVED in 1.1.2)]: the root command rejects it — no caller may rely on bd sync
    pattern: ^[1-9][0-9]*$      (expected a NON-ZERO exit)
    actual:  0

The spec's own diagnostic names the situation exactly:
  "bd 1.2.1 output shape mismatch for 'sync (REMOVED in 1.1.2)' — supported range: >=0.47 <(next-known-break: none recorded — this bd version is the first; update README.md 'Supported bd range' and this spec)"

So the spec is behaving CORRECTLY: it is the version-shape tripwire firing on a bd upgrade that left the pinned range. This is the mechanism working, not failing.

EVIDENCE OF ATTRIBUTION (measured, single writer, tree content-stable):
- Previous full component run, same working tree, bd 1.1.2: `--- bd-compat.sh: PASSED (75 assertion(s) in 54s) ---`
- Later full component run, same working tree, bd 1.2.1: `--- bd-compat.sh: FAILED rc=1 (in 32s) ---`, exactly 1 failing assertion, the `bd sync` row.
- `git status --porcelain .claude/tests/component/specs/bd-compat.sh` => empty (unmodified).
- `git diff -- .claude/ install.sh install.ps1 | grep 'bd sync'` => no matches.

WHAT NEEDS DECIDING (not done here — this is triage, not a fix):
1. Does bd 1.2.1 genuinely re-accept `bd sync`, and if so what does it DO? The v5 plan's "Unplanned P0" section records that 1.1.2 REMOVED it, and that the L2 fixture shim injects `--no-daemon` into every bd call. If `sync` is back, the removal rationale in `session-end.sh` / `beads-ledger.sh` headers should be re-read against 1.2.1 behaviour before anything relies on it again.
2. Update README.md's 'Supported bd range' and the bd-compat pin, per the spec's own instruction.
3. Re-check the other 1.1.2-era migration rows in bd-compat.sh:137-161 against 1.2.1 while in there.

DO NOT simply relax the assertion. The row exists because callers must not rely on `bd sync`; if 1.2.1 restored it, that is a real behaviour change to model, not an expectation to widen.

title: A content-hash restore check is blind to file MODE: two shipped scripts shipped 100755 -> 100644 through ten mutation rounds and every bar
description:
QA round-1 finding R1-F1 on claude-workflow-plugin-s5qf, recorded in the qa-claude review artifact on that task. The INSTANCE was fixed during that review (chmod 755); this task is the PREVENTION, which is the part that outlives it.

THE OBSERVATION. s5qf arrived at QA with both edited scripts at mode 100644 against HEAD's 100755:

    mode change 100755 => 100644 .claude/scripts/verify-before-stop.sh
    mode change 100755 => 100644 .claude/scripts/workflow-manifest.sh

They were the only two of 27 files in .claude/scripts/ not executable. The change was disclosed in no comment, no note and no contract field, and no check in the repo caught it.

WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT, which is the actual defect:

  * The specialist ran ten reddening mutations that rewrote these two files, and
    verified each restore with "every source hash byte-exact after each restore".
    That is sha256 of CONTENT. It is structurally blind to mode, so a mode-lossy
    restore passes it every time.
  * `make test` cannot see it: the only `-x` assertion in the L1 suite targets
    resolve-fixture-spec.sh. Nothing asserts that the SHIPPED hook scripts are
    executable.
  * `make lint` cannot see it: shellcheck does not read modes.
  * The e2e fixture mirrors are NOT a control here — Makefile:400 chmods them
    0755 unconditionally on every `make sync-fixtures`, so the mirrors stay 755
    no matter what the canonical files do. The one place a drift would be
    visible is forced clean.

WHY IT WAS ONLY MEDIUM, so this is not scoped wider than it needs to be. Nothing
breaks today: both hook wirings invoke via `bash "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/..."`
(.claude/settings.json AND .claude/hooks/hooks.json), install.sh:1877 runs
`chmod +x "$TARGET/.claude/scripts/"*.sh` on install, and sync-fixtures forces
0755 on the mirrors. So the gate cannot fail to run and installs are unaffected.
The exposure is a repo artifact: a clone running `./.claude/scripts/workflow-manifest.sh`
directly (the form its own usage header documents) gets permission denied, and
git history would carry an unexplained mode change on the two most critical
scripts in the plugin.

CANDIDATE DIRECTIONS (a decision, not a design):
  * A restore check that compares mode alongside content wherever a mutation
    sweep saves and restores a file. `stat -f %Lp` / `stat -c %a` beside the
    sha256 is the whole fix on the harness side.
  * A cheap L1 leg asserting every `.claude/scripts/*.sh` is mode 0755 in the
    working tree, with a META that reds it. This is the leg that would have
    caught the instance regardless of which tool dropped the bit — worth more
    than the harness fix, because it does not assume the harness was the cause.

NOTE ON ATTRIBUTION: the mechanism was inferred, not observed. Both files carry
an identical mtime (21:18:30) that postdates the last tracked edit, which is
consistent with a final restore step writing both, but the session cannot be
replayed. Whoever picks this up should NOT assume the mutation harness under
.claude/tests/mutation/ is the culprit — it may have been an ad-hoc restore. The
L1 mode assertion is cause-agnostic and is the safer first move.

title: The review-artifact JSON is never written to disk: nine rounds, zero artifact files, arc-wide

or the orchestrator read it from a path that no longer exists. Then make the write observable:

comments.author: username
comments.text:
FIX SPEC + PAIRING, established 2026-08-14 at HEAD 9488c69 by a read-only multi-agent audit with
adversarial verification. Every claim carries the command that produced it. Implement AGAINST THIS,
not against the task title, whose premise is falsified in the preceding comment.

# 3. THE FIX SPEC

Operator directive on `rqer` (`bd show claude-workflow-plugin-rqer`, comment 2026-08-13) sets the shape: *"PERSIST the review artifact to disk at a CANONICAL PATH. REFERENCE IT BY HASH from the bd record… INCLUDE IT IN THE CHANGE SET, so the APPROVAL COVERS IT."* Each criterion below is falsifiable and names what shows it failing.

### AC-1 — Canonical path, derived from the task id, outside `.qa-tracking/`

The artifact's canonical location becomes a committed, task-derived path (proposed `docs/reviews/<task-id>-r<n>.json`; the exact directory is the specialist's to name, the properties are not). It must be *derived*, never supplied — the shipped precedent is `design-record`, whose emitters are at `qa-gate.sh:5508` (`artifact_path_not_derived`) and `qa-gate.sh:5533` (`artifact_outside_spec_dir`), with `design_path_is_contained` closing the symlink-escape arm.

*Fails if:* `qa-gate.sh review-record <tid> --file <any path other than the derived one>` returns `ok:true`. *Fails if:* a symlink at the derived path pointing outside the directory is accepted and hashed.

### AC-2 — Gitignore

Today: `git check-ignore -v .claude/.qa-tracking/review-artifact-x-r1.json` → `.gitignore:12:.claude/.qa-tracking/` (rc=0, ignored). The new location must not be: `git check-ignore -v docs/reviews/x.json` → rc=1 today (not ignored). **No `.gitignore` change is required if the canonical path moves out of `.claude/.qa-tracking/`.** Do not punch a negative pattern into `.gitignore:12` to un-ignore a subpath of the ephemera directory — that directory is also where `changed-files.txt`, `current-task`, iteration counters and the 33 `completion-*.json` payloads live (`ls -1 .../completion-*.json | wc -l` → `33`).

*Fails if:* `git check-ignore -v <canonical path>` exits 0 after the change. *Fails if:* `git status --porcelain` does not list the artifact as untracked/modified after a review round.

### AC-3 — The bd record names the bytes

The `REVIEW-ARTIFACT v1` grammar (`qa-gate.sh:4838`, quoted in §1) gains an `artifact_hash=<64 hex>` token, produced by the same instrument the design side already uses. Verified reproducible:

```
$ bash .claude/scripts/workflow-manifest.sh hash-file .claude/.qa-tracking/review-artifact-…-d2j.2-r1.json
f73ea9624551c3d8f80087c066aeea974520a59eac3242175998d095e62fd001
$ shasum -a 256 <same file>
f73ea9624551c3d8f80087c066aeea974520a59eac3242175998d095e62fd001
```

`cmd_approve` re-hashes the artifact at approve time and carries the token in the approval comment or refuses to claim a binding — mirroring `qa-gate.sh:3763-3788`, where `design_field="design_hash=$recorded_design_hash "` is only set after `live_design_hash == recorded_design_hash`, and every failure arm writes an explicit `WARNING no design binding — …` string instead.

*Fails if:* a `REVIEW-ARTIFACT v1` record exists with no `artifact_hash=` token. *Fails if:* mutating one byte of the artifact after `review-record` and then running `approve` produces an approval that claims a verified binding.

### AC-4 — The artifact enters the change set

Measured today by sourcing `/Users/edk0/Desktop/projects/claude-workflow-plugin/.claude/scripts/workflow-denylist.sh` and calling both predicates:

```
.claude/.qa-tracking/review-artifact-…-0in1-r1.json   denylist=keep  self_written=SELF-WRITTEN
docs/reviews/claude-workflow-plugin-0in1-r1.json      denylist=keep  self_written=keep
docs/specs/claude-workflow-plugin-0in1.md             denylist=keep  self_written=keep
```

`WORKFLOW_SELF_WRITTEN_REGEX` (`workflow-denylist.sh:265`) is `(^|/)\.claude/\.qa-tracking/|(^|/)\.beads/interactions\.jsonl$` — it excludes the *whole directory*, at tracker-write time. Its appliers are `post-edit.sh:178`, `qa-gate.sh:809`, `qa-gate.sh:928`, `verify-before-stop.sh:536`, `verify-before-stop.sh:2048`. Moving the canonical path out of that directory satisfies "include it in the change set" **without weakening the rule at all** — which matters, because `workflow-denylist.sh:249-259` records that this rule *is* the fix for R2-F5 (a reviewer's `.qa-tracking` write moved `change_set_hash`, staled the impact report, and made approve refuse `impact_report_stale`, live at `qa-gate.sh:3164`; it went unnoticed for two review rounds). Relaxing the regex re-opens that bug for every other file in the directory; relocating the artifact does not.

*Fails if:* after a review round, the artifact path is absent from `.claude/.qa-tracking/changed-files.txt`. *Fails if:* the approval comment's `change_set_hash` equals the hash computed over the tracker *without* the artifact path.

### AC-5 — The artifact survives approve

`wipe_review_artifacts` must not match the canonical path. The precedent to copy is stated in-file at `qa-gate.sh:1584-1587` for completion payloads: *"NOT wiped by wipe_review_artifacts and NOT truncated by approve, deliberately: it is the evidence the cross-check below was made against, so it has to outlive the cycle."* The scratch-file wipe of `.qa-tracking` hand-off copies may remain (that is what stops a stale artifact being re-recorded as fresh); the canonical committed copy must not be reachable by any glob in that function.

*Fails if:* driving a full round then `qa-gate.sh approve` leaves the canonical path absent. *Fails if:* `grep -c 'docs/reviews\|<canonical dir>' <the body of wipe_review_artifacts>` is non-zero.

### AC-6 — The circularity is resolved by keeping three tokens separate

The fixpoint is real and measured. `change_set_hash()` is `impact-report.sh:287-289` → `canonical_changed_files | sha256_stdin`, and `canonical_changed_files` (`impact-report.sh:257-271`) emits the denylist-filtered `LC_ALL=C sort -u` **path list** — file contents are never read. So membership alone moves the hash:

```
$ printf '%s\n' ".claude/scripts/qa-gate.sh" "docs/WORKFLOW.md" | LC_ALL=C sort -u | shasum -a 256
dad2638306e4b33d35c4001c3b6b89941786ccf9be93c300f1db953cfc63a952
$ printf '%s\n' ".claude/scripts/qa-gate.sh" "docs/WORKFLOW.md" "docs/reviews/claude-workflow-plugin-0in1-r1.json" | LC_ALL=C sort -u | shasum -a 256
940c53b702eec263ab5012a48954b99c37520461a4e1be05e156562c630963a6
```

Resolution — three tokens, none self-referential:

1. `reviewed_hash` (inside the artifact) keeps naming the **pre-artifact** set: what the reviewer actually read. It is a claim about the past and must not be rewritten.
2. `artifact_hash` (AC-3) is a **byte digest of the artifact file**. The artifact's bytes contain `reviewed_hash` but never `artifact_hash`, so there is no fixpoint.
3. `change_set_hash` on the approval names the **post-artifact** set, which includes the artifact path. The approval attests to a superset of what was reviewed, and says so.

Two shipped refusals sit on this seam and must be handled explicitly, not by loosening them:

- `impact_report_stale` (`qa-gate.sh:3164`) — the impact report must be regenerated after the artifact lands and before `approve`, or approve refuses.
- `expected_hash_mismatch` — `approve --expect-hash` must be given the **post-artifact** hash, or it refuses against the hash the caller classified.

**Out of scope, and this is load-bearing:** the fix may not redefine `change_set_hash`. `git show --stat 9488c69` message: *"What change_set_hash hashes is untouched — that is k0mc, and it lands before D5."* `bd show claude-workflow-plugin-k0mc --json | jq -c '.[0]|{status,priority}'` → `{"status":"open","priority":1}`.

*Fails if:* the artifact's `reviewed_hash` is ever equal to the approval's `change_set_hash` on a task where the artifact is in the change set. *Fails if:* a review round leaves `approve` unable to complete without `--force`-style bypass. *Fails if:* the diff touches `change_set_hash()` or `canonical_changed_files()` in `impact-report.sh`.

---

# 4. THE PAIRING

Per `.claude/tests/README.md:532-577`, a pair is PAIRED only with all four parts: non-vacuity with proof the mutation landed; a specific-misbehaviour assertion naming the check that would fail; a restore control; and **at least one leg observing the shipped artifact running**.

Relevant existing state: leg 4 already exists for "the sol driver writes a file at all" — `.claude/tests/component/specs/codex-review.sh:85-104` drives the shipped `codex-review.sh` against a stub server and asserts `[ -f "$RR_OUT" ]` plus `validate-artifact … .ok == true`. **That leg cannot catch this defect**, because it never runs `approve`. The new pairing must cross the approve boundary.

### Leg A — EXECUTION leg (satisfies part 4)

Drive both shipped scripts end to end in a fixture with `export CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR="$FIXTURE"` (the isolation shape already used by `qa-gate-grade-record.test.sh:163`, `qa-gate-choose.test.sh:136`, `design-artifact.test.sh:126`):

1. Run the shipped `.claude/scripts/codex-review.sh` (stub server, as the component spec already does) **or** the shipped claude-lane path `qa-gate.sh review-record <tid> --file <canonical>`.
2. Assert the canonical path exists and `review-check.sh validate-artifact` returns `.ok == true`.
3. Capture `H0 = workflow-manifest.sh hash-file <canonical>`.
4. Assert the posted `REVIEW-ARTIFACT v1` record contains `artifact_hash=$H0` (AC-3).
5. Assert `<canonical>` appears in `$FIXTURE/.claude/.qa-tracking/changed-files.txt` (AC-4).
6. Run the shipped `qa-gate.sh approve <tid>` to completion; assert exit 0 and `qa-approved` on the task.
7. **Assert the canonical file still EXISTS, and `hash-file` still returns `H0`** (AC-5).
8. Assert the approval comment's `change_set_hash` differs from the hash of the tracker with `<canonical>` removed (AC-6, proves membership rather than asserting it).

Tier: this must land where CI runs it. `make test` is L1 only (`Makefile:49` `test: bash .claude/scripts/tests/run-tests.sh`); the component tier is `make test-component`, and `test-ci` = `test` + `test-component` + `test-e2e-unit` + `manifest-validate` (`Makefile:250-262`). A component spec qualifies; an L1-only spec does not exercise the approve path.

### Leg B — NEGATIVE CONTROL, mutation 1: put the canonical path back in the wipe

Mutant: in a throwaway copy of `qa-gate.sh`, extend the `wipe_review_artifacts` glob at 1060-1062 to cover the canonical directory (or delete the exemption the fix adds).

- **Non-vacuity proof:** `cmp -s mutant shipped && exit 7` — the mutant must differ from the shipped file; plus `bash -n mutant`. If the fix is expressed as a `case`/guard rather than a glob, use an `awk … END { if (!found) exit 7 }` on the stripped construct.
- **Specific misbehaviour, naming the check:** Leg A step 7 must go RED — "the artifact is absent after approve, so the `artifact_hash=$H0` recorded in the bd comment names bytes nothing can produce, and the release-audit citation pattern of `docs/RELEASE_AUDIT.md:469` becomes a dangling path." Not "the mutant is different".
- **Restore control:** Leg A on the shipped script, same fixture, same call shape → step 7 GREEN.

### Leg C — NEGATIVE CONTROL, mutation 2: exclude the artifact from the change set

Mutant: add the canonical directory to `WORKFLOW_SELF_WRITTEN_REGEX` (`workflow-denylist.sh:265`) in a throwaway copy — the exact condition that holds today for `.claude/.qa-tracking/`.

- **Non-vacuity proof:** source the mutant lib and assert `workflow_self_written "<canonical>"` returns 0 while the shipped lib returns 1 (the shipped values are measured above: `keep` for `docs/reviews/…`, `SELF-WRITTEN` for `.claude/.qa-tracking/…`).
- **Specific misbehaviour, naming the check:** Leg A steps 5 and 8 must go RED — "the artifact never reaches `changed-files.txt`, so the approval's `change_set_hash` is computed over a set that excludes the evidence, and the approval attests to nothing about the artifact — the exact 'artifact outside the change set is an artifact no approval attests to' failure the operator directive names."
- **Restore control:** shipped lib, same fixture → steps 5 and 8 GREEN.

Leg A is the execution leg for both mutations. Both mutations must be applied to *copies* in a fixture with `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` redirected — never to the tree.

---

# 5. WHAT REMAINS UNKNOWN

1. **Whether the a9hh review artifacts were ever on disk.** Approve fired twice on that task (06:43:44Z, 10:41:02Z on 2026-08-11) before `rqer` was filed at 11:32:31Z, which is sufficient to explain their absence — but I did not observe the writes. **Experiment:** grep the a9hh-era subagent transcripts under `/Users/edk0/.claude/projects/-Users-edk0-Desktop-projects-claude-workflow-plugin/*/subagents/*.jsonl` for `review-record …a9hh… --file` and for `codex-review.sh … a9hh`, and pair each `tool_use` with its `tool_result` — a `recorded` result on a `--file` invocation proves existence at that instant, exactly as it did for 0in1/nq5f/46w9.

2. **Who wrote the ten `review-request-*-r<n>.json` files.** No shipped producer writes that spelling (`grep -rn 'review-request-[^ "]*-r' .claude/agents .claude/scripts docs LESSONS.md CHANGELOG.md` → no output), so they came from ad-hoc agent commands. **Experiment:** grep the same subagent store for `review-request-` heredocs and `Write` calls, and cross-reference the file mtimes (`a9hh-r1` Aug 10 16:06 local, `mdnc-r2` Aug 14 05:38 local).

3. **UNVERIFIED: whether `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` is set in the root session's Bash environment.** In my own subagent process it is unset (`echo "[${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR-UNSET}]"` → `[UNSET]`), and `jq -r '.env|keys[]' .claude/settings.json` → `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH, CLAUDE_LATEST_OPUS, MAX_THINKING_TOKENS` — not there either; it appears only interpolated into the eight hook command strings. `orchestrator.md:605` invokes the driver as `bash "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/.claude/scripts/codex-review.sh"`, which fails loudly if empty. **Experiment:** run `printenv CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` from a root-session Bash call (not a subagent) and from inside a hook.

4. **UNVERIFIED: whether the unchecked-`mv` fall-through at `codex-review.sh:510` has ever fired in production.** I reproduced the failure shape in an isolated copy; I have no run log showing it in this repo. **Experiment:** add a temporary `mv … || fail_no_artifact` and a `[ -f "$ART_FILE" ]` post-check to a fixture copy, then drive the component spec's C1/C6 legs — or, retrospectively, grep session transcripts for `codex-review exit: 0` followed by a `jq` over the printed path that errored.

5. **UNVERIFIED: whether any allowlisted bare-glob delete was ever exercised.** `.claude/settings.local.json:32` allowlists `"Bash(rm -f *)"`. That is an enabling condition, not a code path, and I established nothing about its use. **Experiment:** grep the transcript store for `rm -f` invocations whose cwd or argument resolves inside `.claude/.qa-tracking/`.

6. **The `d2j.2` survivor's exposure is currently unbounded.** It is `closed` with no `qa-approved`; if a future approve ever completes on that task id, `wipe_review_artifacts "claude-workflow-plugin-d2j.2"` deletes the file cited as PROVEN evidence at `docs/RELEASE_AUDIT.md:469`. I did not establish whether any workflow can still call approve on a closed task. **Experiment:** read `cmd_approve`'s preconditions between 2731 and 3164 for a status guard, and drive `qa-gate.sh approve <closed-tid>` in a fixture.

title: mutation-sweep scores every mutant KILLED: DEFAULT_TEST_CMD is the whole 13.4-min L1 tier but MUTANT_TEST_TIMEOUT_S=60, so the oracle times out before it measures anything
description:
FOUND during QA of a9hh (2026-08-10), while tracing consumers of run-tests.sh. Pre-existing and entirely outside the a9hh change set — filed separately so it is not conflated with it.

THE MECHANISM, three facts that compose:

1. `.claude/tests/mutation/mutation-sweep.sh:317` sets
     DEFAULT_TEST_CMD="bash .claude/scripts/tests/run-tests.sh"
   i.e. the WHOLE L1 tier, not a subset.

2. `.claude/tests/mutation/mutation.conf:41` sets MUTANT_TEST_TIMEOUT_S=60, and
   mutation-sweep.sh:431 wraps the oracle in it:
     CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR="$wt" timeout_cmd "$MUTANT_TEST_TIMEOUT_S" bash -c "$TEST_CMD"

3. mutation-sweep.sh:434 classifies by exit status alone:
     if [ "$test_rc" -eq 0 ]; then  # survived
   so a timeout (rc=124) is scored KILLED.

MEASURED: the full L1 tier is 804s = 13.4 minutes (sum of per-spec elapsed, 36 specs, this repo at 535c89a+a9hh). Against a 60s cap the oracle can never complete, so every mutant exits non-zero and is recorded KILLED regardless of whether the mutation was detectable. A mutation score of 100% is then indistinguishable from an oracle that never ran — the same shape as a9hh, in a different harness.

NOT MEASURED BY ME: I did not run a sweep, so I have not observed a false KILLED end to end. The three facts above are read from source and the 13.4-min figure is measured. Reproduce with a single mutant and check whether the recorded test_rc is 124.

ALSO NOTE the doc/code mismatch: `.claude/tests/mutation/README.md:58` describes the default as "the L1 unit subset ... That keeps the sweep fast", and mutation.conf:27 repeats "the harness defaults to the L1 unit subset". There is no subset — DEFAULT_TEST_CMD is the entire tier. Either the default should become a genuine fast subset (and the docs stay true), or MUTANT_TEST_TIMEOUT_S must exceed the tier's real runtime with margin, or the sweep must distinguish rc=124 from a genuine test failure and refuse to score a mutant whose oracle timed out.

FIX DIRECTION: at minimum, make a timed-out oracle a THIRD outcome that is never KILLED — the same correction a9hh applied to run-tests.sh, where the timeout is now a FAILED-with-distinct-reason rather than being folded into a pass/fail binary.

RELATED: a9hh (skip/timeout as distinct outcomes in the tier runners), mwrb (the per-spec caps).

title: PRODUCT DECISION: should review-config ship max_review_iterations=12 and timeout_seconds=2400 as defaults? Raised by the orchestrator to unblock a Sol lane; both installers copy the file to every target
description:
SPLIT OUT OF fkm.1.11 at the grader's requirement (rubric v2, C4+C5 fail) and QA's R9-F1. The change is currently REVERTED in that change set; this task owns the decision.

WHAT HAPPENED: to run a Sol/Codex review on fkm.1.11 I edited .claude/review-config via sed from the orchestrator — max_review_iterations 3 -> 12, timeout_seconds 300 -> 2400 — on the operator's instruction ('300s is too small for sol, make at least 40mins limit'). install.sh:2668 and install.ps1:2680 COPY THAT FILE TO EVERY TARGET, so both values would ship as product defaults: a 40-minute wall-clock budget on a paid API, and four times the permitted Codex turns per change set. The file's own header calls it THE ONE PLACE caps live. No in-file rationale, no CHANGELOG entry, no test coverage — the L2 spec writes its own config, so the shipped values are asserted by nothing.

THE MEASUREMENT THAT SHOULD DRIVE THIS DECISION, and it contradicts the premise the instruction was given on: THE 300s TIMEOUT WAS NEVER THE BLOCKER. Sol completed a real 1008-line scoped review payload in 66 SECONDS — inside the ORIGINAL budget — producing a schema-valid artifact with a genuine HIGH that six same-family review rounds had missed. What actually blocked the first attempt was max_review_iterations=3, returning rc=6 at ZERO seconds. I reported the timeout as the cause before measuring it; the operator's instruction was reasonable given my report and the report was wrong.

SO THE TWO VALUES HAVE DIFFERENT EVIDENCE:
- timeout_seconds 2400: NOT supported by any measurement here. 66s of 300 was used. Raising it asserts something no observation supports. If it should rise, the case must come from a payload that actually exhausted 300.
- max_review_iterations 12: the limit that DID fire, and nq5f now records the real defect — THE COUNTER DOES NOT DISTINGUISH CODEX TURNS FROM CLAUDE ONES, so a change set that has had several Claude rounds becomes permanently ineligible for a Codex turn. That is the task most in need of a second model family being structurally excluded from it. Raising the cap treats the symptom; making the counter lane-aware treats the defect.

RECOMMENDATION: fix nq5f (lane-aware counting) rather than shipping a higher cap, and leave timeout_seconds at 300 until a measurement justifies otherwise. If either value does ship, it needs an in-file rationale, a CHANGELOG entry, and an L2 leg asserting the SHIPPED values rather than a spec-authored config.

RELATED: nq5f (the lane-blind counter, premise corrected), fkm.1.11 (where this rode in).
notes:
COMPLETED (devops): caps ship (12/2400) with all three grader conditions: in-file rationale carrying the 66s-of-300 measurement + rc=6-at-zero-seconds + lane-blind counter (nq5f, revisit-down note); CHANGELOG [Unreleased] entry; L2 section C8 asserting the SHIPPED bytes — iteration cap bracketed behaviourally at the rc=6 boundary (12 admitted, 13 refused), timeout pinned via read_cap extracted verbatim from the shipped driver, drifted-config negative control (assert_mutant_applied) reproducing the pre-iu5o refusal + restore control. J26 CONFIG disposition recorded in comments. Validated: codex-review spec 66/66 in 16s through the shipped L2 runner.
IN PROGRESS: none — rides the a9hh gate.
KEY DECISIONS: C1-C7 keep spec-authored fixture configs (they test cap MECHANICS); C8 alone owns shipped-value assertions — the separation is the point.
close_reason: Shipped in bd377f5 on v5/design-phase. Ten review rounds across two model families (sol-codex, qa-claude), seventeen findings, all fixed and independently re-verified. Approved at change_set_hash 33ddc1c7 (the earlier 19-path set at 668b8d19). Measured at bd377f5: L1 36/36/0/0 Partial 0 with 2677 assertions and the completeness floor HELD; make lint rc=0; shellcheck on the L2 runner rc=0 separately; L3 451p/5s/0f; L2 44 specs 43 passed 1 failed Partial 1, 2928/2, sole red the PRE-EXISTING installer-v3-upgrade 8e-B proven at pristine 535c89a. Linux evidence is an ubuntu:24.04/bash 5.2.21/aarch64 container; GitHub-hosted x86_64 remains UNMEASURED and the rewired l1-unit job's first push is its first measurement.

- CONFIG (the module that applies): raises two defaults for the OPTIONAL, ADVISORY Sol lane only; the Claude review path and the qa-gate release credential are structurally unaffected (caps are read at exactly one non-test site, codex-review.sh:119-120). title: record_verification coerces a non-numeric exit code to 0 with tr -cd, so a malformed rc is reported as 'exited 0' — the same degrade-to-a-constant model, one function over, and silent
description:
RAISED BY THE ROUND-5 DEVOPS SPECIALIST ON fkm.1.11, DISAGREEING WITH MY SCOPING, AND IT IS RIGHT. I scoped R4-F7 out as cosmetic. Its objection, verbatim: 'I left R4-F7 alone per your scoping, but I disagree it is cosmetic: tr -cd 0-9 coercing a non-numeric rc to 0 is the same model failure one function over, and a silent one, since the readout then prints exited 0.'

THE MECHANISM: record_verification (verify-before-stop.sh) sanitises its rc argument with tr -cd '0-9' and defaults an empty result to 0. So a caller passing a non-numeric exit code — a shell variable that did not expand, a signal name, an error string — has it silently rewritten to the value that means SUCCESS. The ledger then records it, and broader_verification_note prints 'exited 0' over a run that did not succeed.

WHY IT IS THE SAME DEFECT AND NOT A SEPARATE ONE: fkm.1.11's rounds 3, 4 and 5 were all one shape — AN INPUT SILENTLY DEGRADES TO A CONSTANT AND NOTHING REFUSES IT. That was fixed at model level inside tree_fingerprint with a single invariant: every producer must exit 0 and every value must have the right shape. record_verification sits in the same file, feeds the same readout, and has the identical hole. The invariant stopped at the function boundary.

THE DIRECTION MATTERS: coercion to 0 is coercion TOWARD SUCCESS. A malformed rc becomes an assertion that the broader verification passed. That is the critical direction by the repo's own severity rule — announcing success over the input it exists to catch — not the noise direction.

FIX DIRECTION: apply the same treatment the invariant uses. A shape test (rc must match ^[0-9]+$), refuse rather than sanitise, and if it cannot be established record it as unknown rather than as 0. Do NOT extend tr to accept more characters — the bjx lesson applies: reject, never sanitise. Whatever ships needs a control that fails when the guard is removed, per the pairing convention this same batch just wrote.

FILED SEPARATELY rather than folded into fkm.1.11 because that change set has run five review rounds and is at +4570/-147; adding a sixth surface to it is how a batch stops being reviewable. This is the post-close-finding convention applied prospectively — a new surface opens a new task.

title: The orchestrator's own busy-check idiom is a false-BUSY machine: pgrep -f matches sibling agent shells running the same check, so it cannot come back clear for a non-author agent
description:
FOUND by the round-3 devops specialist on fkm.1.11, 2026-08-08. THE DEFECT IS IN AN INSTRUCTION THE ORCHESTRATOR WROTE INTO EVERY SPECIALIST AND QA BRIEF THIS SESSION.

THE IDIOM, handed to ~8 agents today as the guard against measurement contention:
  pgrep -f 'component/run.sh|run-tests|vitest|make test'

THE DEFECT: pgrep -f matches FULL COMMAND LINES. It excludes its own invoker but NOT sibling agent shells. Every agent shell that runs this check carries the pattern in its own argv, so concurrent agents see each other and report BUSY. The specialist measured its own check sitting BUSY on FOUR such wrapper shells long after the real runners had exited.

ITS OWN WORDS, which name the class exactly: A CHECK THAT CAN NEVER FIRE LOOKS IDENTICAL TO ONE STILL WAITING.

STATUS OF VERIFICATION, stated precisely because this task is about not overclaiming: the orchestrator ran the check immediately after and got CLEAR both for the broad pattern and for a narrowed real-runner pattern - but no other agent shells existed at that moment, so the condition was absent and the negative result is not a refutation. The mechanism is sound and the orchestrator could not falsify it. Reproduce with two concurrent agents both running the check.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN ITS SIZE: this check was introduced to PREVENT contention-induced false measurements, after eight such incidents this session (mrd2). A false BUSY makes an agent wait forever or skip a tier it should have run, and it fails exactly when multiple agents are active - which is the only time it matters. The guard against false measurement is itself a false measurement, in the orchestrator's own tooling.

CANDIDATE FIXES, none obviously right:
- Match the RUNNER PROCESSES rather than the pattern string: pgrep -f 'bash .claude/scripts/tests/run-tests.sh|bash .claude/tests/component/run.sh' - narrower, still string-based, still matchable by a shell that types it.
- A lock file written by the runners themselves, checked by everyone else. The runner writes it, so the check cannot be fooled by someone merely NAMING the runner. Same principle as the verification ledger this batch just built: the command records its own state.
- Have the orchestrator own all tier runs (already the practice) and drop the check from specialist briefs entirely, replacing it with 'do not run L2/L3'.

SECOND MACHINE FACT from the same specialist, worth its own line: L1 takes over 10 minutes on this machine and the Bash tool's maximum foreground timeout is 600000ms, so a FOREGROUND make test is guaranteed to be SIGTERMed mid-suite. The orchestrator's bar runs were all backgrounded and so never hit it; a specialist told to run make test in the foreground will be killed partway and see a truncated log. That belongs in the brief template too.

RELATED: mrd2 (the contention class this check exists to guard), 71gw (every number carries the command that produced it).

title: bd comments --json would DECIDE the 0.47 comment-availability unknown instead of betting on it — named in the fkm.1.18 filing, absent from the shipped code
description:
QA round-1 finding R1-F2 on rmz (medium, non-blocking), recorded in the qa-claude review artifact.

THE SHIPPED FIX uses comment_count as the witness for whether comments are available, giving three states (verified / unverified / unavailable) and failing CLOSED when it cannot tell. Correct as far as it goes, and QA agreed with fail-closed.

THE REDUCIBLE PART: 'bd comments <id> --json' EXISTS on 1.1.2. It returns []/rc=0 on a genuinely-zero task and full bodies otherwise. So it DECIDES the case the current design declares unknowable. The original fkm.1.18 filing NAMED it - the filing says 'bd comment list' - and it appears NOWHERE in the shipped code, the implementation notes, or the F7 contract. Neither used nor rejected in writing. An option named in the filing and silently dropped is the gap, independent of whether adopting it is right.

WHY IT MATTERS MOST FOR bd_doc_write: on a bd 0.47 that omits or nulls the comments key, the current guard refuses - so the orchestrator cannot write a SPEC doc on a fresh task. QA's point: Go marshals a nil slice as null, so a 0.47 install hitting this is closer to a coin flip than a remote edge.

THE SPECIALIST'S OWN LARGEST UNKNOWN was exactly this: whether bd 0.47.x publishes comment_count. Only 1.1.2 is installed so it could not test. This task is how we stop guessing.

DELIVERABLE: either wire the decider in where available, or record in writing why it was rejected. Do not leave it neither used nor rejected. Whatever ships needs a control that fails when the decider is removed.

title: MCP servers hold STALE CODE for the life of a session: a fix to an MCP tool is not live until the server restarts, and nothing surfaces the version skew
description:
DISCOVERED while fixing fkm.1.18, 2026-08-08, and it is the REASON fkm.1.18 looked like a code defect when it was not.

THE TIMELINE, measured: fdfd6ce (2026-08-03) fixed the bd-mcp comments transport, touching exec-bd.js and bd_comment.js. fkm.1.18 was filed 2026-08-04 - ONE DAY LATER - reporting mcp__bd__bd_list_comments returning ok:true with 0 comments on a task carrying 76. The specialist drove the ON-DISK handler directly and got 88 comments on the same task. The on-disk code was correct the whole time.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED: the running MCP server process was started before fdfd6ce and served stale code for the rest of the session. The process is gone, so this cannot be proven now - the specialist said so plainly rather than claiming it. But the timeline is not in dispute and no other explanation fits the evidence.

CONFIRMED STILL TRUE RIGHT NOW: the specialist reports the running bd MCP server is STILL old code, so neither of today's fixes (rmz label suppression, fkm.1.18 three-state comments) is live for mcp__bd__* tools in this session until the server restarts. It used the bd CLI throughout for exactly this reason.

WHY THIS IS ITS OWN TASK AND NOT A NOTE:

1. It cost a P1 filing with a wrong root cause, and I wrote that wrong root cause into a specialist brief. The correction only surfaced because the specialist checked the premise instead of taking it.

2. It is the claimed-but-unverified family in a new place. A fix that is committed, tested green, and NOT RUNNING is indistinguishable from a fix that works - the tests pass because they drive the on-disk code, while every agent in the session gets the old behaviour. The test suite and the live surface disagree and nothing reports the disagreement.

3. It will recur every time we fix an MCP tool. Both MCP servers ship with this plugin. D1/D2 add design-artifact readers that may reach MCP surfaces, so v5 adds instances.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY HELP, none of which is obviously right:
- a version or build stamp in every MCP tool response, so a stale server is visible in its own output;
- a SessionStart check comparing the running server's stamp against the on-disk source hash, warning on skew (never blocking - the never-block invariant holds);
- documenting the restart requirement where agents will hit it, which is the cheap half.

RELATED: fkm.1.18 (the original, root cause corrected on that task), rmz (same commit).

title: The root-orchestrated relay - the plugin structural answer to subagents-cannot-spawn-subagents - has NO behavioural assertion at any tier; three layers each defer to the next
description:
FOUND by the negative-control census (iexi). The census called this zero negative control and the single worst structural gap. THAT OVERSTATES IT and I am correcting the claim while keeping the finding, because the accurate version is what determines the fix.

WHAT IS NOT TRUE: the five relay sentinel checks in no-nested-spawn-instructions.test.sh:84-100 are NOT vacuous in the removal direction. They assert grep exit status 0, and grep returns 1 when the string is absent, so deleting a relay anchor from a prompt DOES turn them red. A presence grep fires on removal by construction.

WHAT IS TRUE, MEASURED 2026-08-07 across three tiers, all files uncontaminated by concurrent edits:

L1 - the five checks verify STRING PRESENCE IN A PROMPT FILE. RUBRIC-RELAY: status=needs-grading, RUBRIC-RELAY: grading-relay, JUDGE-RELAY: judging-relay, REVIEW-RELAY: status=needs-review, REVIEW-RELAY: review-relay. That a prompt CONTAINS a literal is not evidence that the relay it describes WORKS. The META-TEST at :276 asserts only that the checker flags a fixture carrying a nested-spawn directive - it proves the SPAWN-DIRECTIVE DETECTOR is sensitive, and says nothing about the five presence checks.

L2 - rubric-loop.sh:50-58 FORMALLY DELEGATES rather than testing: the handoff is a prompt-level contract enforced via the L1 sentinel test no-nested-spawn-instructions.test.sh, and the script-level surface exercised below is invariant under where the grader spawn fires from. So L2 states outright that it does not distinguish the thing the relay exists to guarantee.

L3 - the same L2 comment cites corroboration: observed end-to-end in the live rubric-revision-loop fixture. The fixture EXISTS (.claude/tests/e2e/fixtures/rubric-revision-loop). But grep over every fixture.yaml invariants block for relay or RELAY returns NOTHING. No fixture DECLARES a relay invariant. Observed was a one-time human observation, not a standing assertion, and nothing re-checks it on any run.

NET: each tier points at another tier, and the chain terminates in a grep for a string. The plugin architecture rests on subagents cannot spawn subagents (documented in CLAUDE.md known antipatterns, citing code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents) with the root-orchestrated relay as the answer. Nothing anywhere asserts that answer behaves correctly.

WHY P2 AND NOT P1: the failure mode is not a silent release. A broken relay produces a visibly stuck workflow - the grader never runs, the rubric label never resolves - rather than an unreviewed change set escaping. Loud failure, not quiet success. It is filed because a three-tier deferral chain ending in a string grep is exactly the structure that hides a real defect, not because a specific defect is known to be present.

FIX DIRECTION: one behavioural assertion at the tier that can afford it, driving the relay shape rather than reading it - QA returns needs-grading, the packet doc lands, a root-level spawn consumes it - plus a declared invariant on the rubric-revision-loop fixture so it is checked every run rather than observed once. Do NOT add a sixth string grep.

title: STANDING INSTRUCTION from the operator: after D2 closes, re-measure the finding rate per phase and report the number
description: Recorded as a task so it survives compaction and session boundaries. The operator instruction verbatim: after D2 closes, re-measure the finding rate per phase; if the negative-control work has not moved it, bring me the number and we cut the remaining D-phases rather than continuing at this rate. WHAT THIS REQUIRES: a defined denominator agreed BEFORE D2 closes, so the comparison is not retrofitted to look favourable. Phase P baseline to beat, measured across P0-P9: roughly 26 recorded instances of the claimed-but-unverified class, across shipped code, specs, plans, agent prompts, the bd CLI, and the orchestrator own reporting. The metric must count findings per phase on a consistent basis; state the basis when reporting. THIS IS A DECISION GATE, NOT A METRIC FOR ITS OWN SAKE — the operator has attached a consequence to it, which is cutting the remaining D-phases.

title: Test-runner contention across tiers: 1nz's CLASS survived its own fix — review-separation.test.sh red under a concurrent L2, 60/60 alone
description: SIXTH INSTANCE, measured 2026-08-07. P5 narrowed workflow-doctor.test.sh snapshot_live because that was the KNOWN instance. The class is wider. The Stop hook L1 run reported review-separation.test.sh FAILING while QA drove component/run.sh --filter installer-v3-upgrade (PIDs 82016/82018/82098). Re-run alone: PASSED 60 assertions, zero failures. review-separation.test.sh drives the real qa-gate.sh against live bd records, so any concurrent bd-record writer perturbs it. ALSO measured the same session: two full L2 attempts died after ONE spec each under the same contention, exit 1 reading as a test failure rather than a kill. THE COST IS THE POINT: a red that is not a regression teaches everyone to re-run rather than believe, and the re-run habit is what eventually waves a real regression through. Twice in one session I had to hand-distinguish contention from failure. CANDIDATE FIXES, neither trivial: a lock between the L1 and L2 runners (P5 rejected a lock because it cannot stop a NON-test writer, still true, but two test runners are exactly the case a lock CAN stop), or fixture-local bd workspaces for specs that touch live records, mirroring what the component tier already does for .beads. Second is durable and larger than a Phase P item. NOTE ON PROVENANCE: this was first recorded as a comment on 1nz AFTER 1nz was closed, where it would never surface in a ready-work query. That mistake is the reason the post-close-finding convention task exists.

comments.author: username
comments.text:
SEVENTH INSTANCE, 2026-08-07 — AND I CAUSED THIS ONE, by the same reasoning that made me file this task.

I ran the negative-control census (iexi) as a parallel workflow against the live tree while a specialist was actively editing it. I justified that explicitly: the census is strictly read-only, so it is safe to parallelise.

READ-ONLY WAS THE WRONG SAFETY PROPERTY. A census whose OUTPUT IS A POPULATION CLAIM needs the tree to be STABLE, not merely un-mutated by itself. Measured contamination: seven files moved under it mid-run - qa.md, qa-gate.sh, verify-before-stop.sh, specs/verify-before-stop.sh, docs/HOOKS.md, docs/WORKFLOW.md, plus a NEW untracked file doc-only-classifier.test.sh created by the specialist after the census inventory phase had completed.

THE CONSEQUENCE IS INSTRUCTIVE AND IS THE CENSUSED DEFECT ITSELF. The census found doc-only-classifier.test.sh in a later phase, could not find it in its own inventory, and concluded it had a POPULATION-LOGIC defect - its self-report says the census skipped the file guarding auto-approval and did not know it had. That conclusion is WRONG. It did not skip the file. The file did not exist when the inventory ran. The census reasoned from an ABSENCE to a CAUSE without checking whether the tree had moved, which is the same shape as the family it was commissioned to measure.

WHAT THIS ADDS TO THE TASK: the contention class is not limited to two TEST RUNNERS racing. It covers any MEASUREMENT taken over a tree that a writer is concurrently changing, including read-only analysis. The durable fix must therefore cover measurement generally, not just test-runner mutual exclusion - e.g. census-type work runs against a git worktree pinned at a commit, never the live tree. That is cheap and would have prevented this entirely.

comments.author: username
comments.text:
**Partial mitigation landed under claude-workflow-plugin-gsfd (the lease, member 5) — the fuller fix this task names (fixture-local bd workspaces) remains OPEN and out of scope here.**

Both candidate fixes this task floats were "neither trivial." gsfd builds the smaller one: `.claude/scripts/tree-lease.sh`, a shared ownership primitive (acquire/heartbeat/release/conflicts/reclaim-stale) sourced by both L1 (`run-tests.sh`) and L2 (`.claude/tests/component/run.sh`) runners AND the Stop hook. Each acquires a lease naming its own tier/label/pid/host/start-time at startup and checks for a LIVE lease from the OTHER tier, printing a loud `CONCURRENT-RUN NOTICE` if one is found — before any spec runs.

This does **not** eliminate the contention this task documents (review-separation.test.sh reading real bd records perturbed by a concurrent L2 run can still happen) — it makes the contention **attributable in one read** instead of the re-run-and-hope habit the task's own text warns costs a real regression eventually: "a red that is not a regression teaches everyone to re-run rather than believe."

A genuine lock (the OTHER candidate, "a lock between the L1 and L2 runners... two test runners are exactly the case a lock CAN stop") was deliberately NOT built here — a real mutual-exclusion mechanism with correct timeout/deadlock handling is a larger, riskier piece of work than this task's slice of gsfd could responsibly absorb alongside everything else in that batch, and rushing it risked introducing a NEW contention-shaped defect. Recorded as a deliberate scope decision, not an oversight.

Automated, paired coverage: `runner-completeness.test.sh` section 16 (11 assertions) — the notice fires when a live lease from the other tier exists (both directions, L1-sees-L2 and L2-sees-L1), stays silent when there is none (restore control), correctly treats a STALE (dead-pid) lease as reclaimed rather than a conflict, and a META-TEST proves the notice genuinely depends on the lease-acquire region (excising it silences the notice even over the SAME live-conflict fixture). Section 16 is green on the latest full run.

The DURABLE fix this task names — fixture-local bd workspaces for record-touching specs like review-separation.test.sh, mirroring what the component tier already does for `.beads` — remains open, unstarted, and is correctly sized here as "larger than a Phase P item." Not closing this task; leaving it open with this comment as the current state of the mitigation.

Files: `.claude/scripts/tree-lease.sh` (new), `.claude/scripts/tests/tree-lease.test.sh` (new), `.claude/scripts/tests/run-tests.sh`, `.claude/tests/component/run.sh`, `.claude/scripts/verify-before-stop.sh`, `.claude/scripts/tests/runner-completeness.test.sh` (section 16).

comments.author: username
comments.text:
A SECOND, STRUCTURALLY DIFFERENT contention shape observed repeatedly across the v5 arc (2026-08-19..22), worth recording here since this task already owns cross-tier contention. This one is not tier-vs-tier — it is THE STOP GATE'S OWN VERIFICATION vs THE MANDATORY QA STEP, and both are compulsory parts of the same workflow.

MECHANISM: verify-before-stop.sh runs the full L1 tier on turn-end whenever the tree has moved. The QA role must write to Beads to do its job — qa-gate.sh enter, impact-report regeneration, review-record, approve. run-tests.sh arms a store canary that fails any spec during whose window the protected store advances. So the gate's test run and QA's writes cannot coexist, and the gate fires automatically rather than on request.

MEASURED INSTANCES (each cost one wasted gate iteration; every one was a canary trip, never an assertion failure, floor HELD every time):
  - design-review-record.test.sh  — store advanced by 3 commits mid-spec
  - design-artifact.test.sh       — by 1 commit (twice, on separate runs)
  - design-conform.test.sh        — by 1 commit
  - gate-claim-honesty.test.sh    — by 4 commits
  - grilling-record.test.sh       — by 2 commits
Attributions named tasks including claude-workflow-plugin-vsue and -dvfr — i.e. writes by the orchestrator's own agents, not a third party. One instance was traced to the ORCHESTRATOR filing a task and immediately resuming an agent that started a tier; the canary caught its own operator.

WHAT IS ALREADY CORRECT AND MUST NOT BE 'FIXED': the canary's hedge is exactly right. It reports that the store ADVANCED DURING the spec's window, never that the spec advanced it — reachability, not authorship. Every instance above was correctly diagnosed from that wording, and the isolated re-runs came back clean (design-artifact 266/266, design-conform 106/106 and later 183/183). Do not weaken the hedge; it is what makes these diagnosable.

WHY IT IS WORTH FIXING ANYWAY: the workflow currently requires a human-or-orchestrator convention ('never write to bd while a tier is in flight') that three specialist agents and the orchestrator itself all violated at least once despite explicit written warnings — the same cadence-vs-convention problem as claude-workflow-plugin-5vv2. A convention that must be obeyed by every concurrent actor, with a 50-minute feedback loop, is not a mechanism.

CANDIDATE DIRECTIONS (not prescriptive): have the canary consult the tree-lease that claude-workflow-plugin-gsfd shipped, so a spec can NAME the lease-holding writer instead of reporting an anonymous advance (the lease is report-only and already carries owner identity — this is the attribution use it was built for and then never wired to); or have run-tests.sh take an advisory lease that qa-gate.sh's write paths check and briefly defer on; or narrow the canary's protected window to the specs that actually read the production store.

PAIRING NOTE: whatever lands must keep a leg proving the canary still FAILS on a genuine in-spec contamination — the risk in 'making the canary smarter' is turning a real detector into a suppressor.

comments.author: username
comments.text:
ESCALATION of the gate-vs-specialist shape recorded earlier in this task: the contention has now caused a genuine SPEC TIMEOUT, not merely a store-canary trip.

OBSERVED 2026-08-24 on claude-workflow-plugin-xsu1, reported by the implementing specialist from its own process inspection:
  - Its round-3 'make test' logged design-conform.test.sh TIMING OUT: 900s per-spec cap, 924s elapsed. That spec was untouched by the round in progress and has no reason to be slow on its own (it runs ~350s uncontended).
  - While investigating, it found a SECOND concurrent 'make test' alive, parented by verify-before-stop.sh (PID 9510) — the Stop hook's own gate verification, which fires automatically on turn-end.
  - Two full L1 tiers were therefore contending for the same .beads store and the same CPU. Both were still alive at its last check, its own run stalled on design-review-record.test.sh with no log growth for 13+ minutes.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN THE CANARY CASE ALREADY RECORDED HERE. A canary trip is diagnosable: the wording names an unattributed store advance and an isolated re-run clears it. A per-spec TIMEOUT is not diagnosable from its own output — 'killed at the 900s cap' reads identically whether the spec hung on its own logic or was simply starved. The runner is right to fail loudly rather than skip (that is claude-workflow-plugin-mwrb's fix working), but the operator cannot tell a real hang from contention without going outside the test output to process inspection, which is exactly what the specialist had to do.

A SECOND, SHARPER OBSERVATION worth recording separately: the orchestrator reported the machine as IDLE, based on pgrep, at a moment when the specialist's own ps and log-mtime checks showed BOTH runs alive. The specialist reported the discrepancy rather than trusting the orchestrator's signal — correctly. Verified afterwards: the orchestrator's pgrep pattern had matched only its own command line, and the process picture from 'ps -axo pid,ppid,etime,args' is the reliable read. So 'is the machine busy?' is itself a measurement this workflow gets wrong, which matters because every anti-contention convention in this project depends on answering it correctly first.

The specialist also declined to kill PID 9510 — not its process, and insufficient visibility into what depended on its completion. That was the right call and is worth preserving as the norm: an agent should not kill a gate run it did not start.

Bearing on the candidate directions already listed above: this strengthens the case for having the runner CONSULT the tree-lease that claude-workflow-plugin-gsfd shipped rather than for making the canary smarter. A lease-aware runner could name the other holder in the timeout message ('killed at cap; another L1 tier held a lease for 41m of this window'), which converts an undiagnosable timeout into a diagnosable one without weakening the cap.

title: qa.md:196 states .claude/.qa-tracking/ is NOT denylisted — 94d's SELF-WRITTEN-FILTER filters it, so QA is steered away from the prescribed artifact path
description:
Found by QA during P7's approval, 2026-08-07, verified with a control and empirically.

qa.md:196 tells QA that .claude/.qa-tracking/ is NOT denylisted. That was true before 94d. It is false now: the SELF-WRITTEN-FILTER added in 94d (post-edit.sh:178) filters that directory, so artifacts QA writes there never enter the change set.

WHY IT MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING A STALE SENTENCE: qa.md is the operating manual for the agent that writes review artifacts, and the sentence steers QA's expectations about the prescribed artifact path. An agent that believes its artifact will be tracked, and finds it is not, will reasonably conclude something is broken — or worse, will relocate its artifacts somewhere that IS tracked, putting review byproducts into the change set under review.

Pre-existing and out of P7's scope. Fix is one sentence, but check for sibling claims in the same section before editing — this class has recurred all arc, and the correct anchor is the SELF-WRITTEN-FILTER sentinel rather than a line number.

RELATED CLARIFICATION FROM THE SAME REVIEW, worth folding in: the 21 declared-but-unbound files in P7's cross-check are sync-fixtures byte-copies, and the completion_files_crosscheck header explains them as 'invisible to post-edit'. QA found a cleaner and stronger explanation — they are DENYLISTED OUTRIGHT, so they can never enter a change set by any route, not merely by that one. Correcting the header to say so would make the reasoning exact.

title: qa-gate.sh approve has no read-only mode — the only way to ask what it would do is to make it act
description:
RAISED 2026-08-06 after the orchestrator ran 'qa-gate.sh approve' on a live task mid-implementation to read an error key. It refused on an unrelated stale impact report, so nothing was written — but with a fresh report and a completion record present that command would have approved the orchestrator's own delegated work with no independent review. The refusal was luck, not procedure.

EVERY OTHER DESTRUCTIVE PATH IN THIS REPO HAS A READ-ONLY MODE: worktree-sweep.sh defaults to dry-run and requires --apply; beads-ledger.sh reconcile requires --apply; qa-gate.sh reconcile-tracker reports before writing. approve is the most consequential write in the system and is the exception.

WHY IT IS NOT A SMALL ADDITION — the P7 specialist investigated and declined to smuggle it in, with this reasoning: reconcile_tracker runs BEFORE the refusals and APPENDS to changed-files.txt. So a --dry-run that got far enough to report what the refusals would say would ALREADY have mutated the change set it was asked about. An honest read-only mode therefore requires giving reconcile_tracker its own read-only mode first — and that is a load-bearing helper with four callers, added in 94d and hardened in 94d.1.

THAT ORDERING IS THE WHOLE TASK: reconcile read-only first, then approve --dry-run on top of it. Doing it the other way round produces a dry-run that lies about the state it inspected, which is the defect family this phase has recorded twenty-four times.

VALUE BEYOND THE ONE INCIDENT: agents and operators need to ask 'why is this refusing' constantly — that is most of what the last two days consisted of. Today the only way to ask is to invoke the irreversible action and read the error, which means the diagnostic path and the approval path are the same command. A --dry-run would also make approve's refusal chain testable from the outside without a fixture, which is currently only reachable through the component harness.

NOT URGENT, and deliberately not folded into P7 — the specialist was right to name it rather than add it unasked.

title: P7: runtime contract validation at approve — validate-completion, completion-record, and a COMPLETION-CONTRACT-REFUSAL in cmd_approve
description:
Phase P item P7, per docs/plans/v5-design-phase.md. Three pieces, each mirroring an existing one, ALL landing at approve (correction 5: enter is documented tolerant and F1 invokes it on classes with no completion payload, so a refusal there deadlocks every doc-only Stop).

1. review-check.sh validate-completion <file> — mirrors cmd_validate_artifact: required-key loop over the canonical seven, the control-character scan over grammar-bearing scalars only, per-field type checks, emit_validate. Introduces NO reviewer/lane reference so reviewer-lane-degradation.sh's structural-purity test still passes.

2. qa-gate.sh completion-record <tid> [--file <path>] — mirrors cmd_review_record including the subprocess call to the ONE validator. Grammar: COMPLETION v1 task=<tid> role=<r> fields=<csv> payload_sha=<sha256> at <ts>: <n> file(s), <m> test(s). THE bjx GRAMMAR-INJECTION CLASS APPLIES: every interpolated scalar must match ^[A-Za-z0-9._+-]+$ — reject, never sanitise. The four free-form fields are never interpolated, only their presence and the payload digest.

3. A refusal in cmd_approve inside # COMPLETION-CONTRACT-REFUSAL BEGIN/END, sited after REVIEW-SEPARATION, with an audited --no-completion '<reason>' bypass parsed in the same loop as --no-impact-report / --no-review. F1 passes --no-completion 'F1 <class> fast path: no specialist, no completion payload'.

LAND BOTH HALVES TOGETHER — the four specialist prompts and qa.md gain the call as their last action, or the refusal fires on every flow.

TESTS: L1 — REWRITE the HONEST CEILING paragraph in completion-contract-parity.test.sh; this change makes its verbatim text false and that file is the repo's own record of what is enforced. New section asserts each carrier names the invocation. L2 specs/qa-gate.sh: valid payload records and approves; missing_key:context_coverage; newline in role -> scalar_contains_control_char; a crafted role containing ': ' rejected by the char class, with the injection reproduction as the leg's NAME; no record -> approve refuses; --no-completion '' exits 1. META: strip the sentinels, assert approve succeeds with no record.

VERIFY: grep -c completion .claude/scripts/qa-gate.sh -> non-zero (it is ZERO today).

FOLD IN fkm.1.20 (P1): the freshness check detects DRIFT but not LOSS, because it compares two reads of the same source. The F7 contract's files_changed is the cheapest INDEPENDENT witness and this is the natural landing site — cross-check the bound change set against it. Would have caught 94d.1's 6-of-8 loss immediately.
notes:

worktree-approval-resolution.sh — PURE MIGRATION GAP, confirmed by measurement not inference. ORCHESTRATOR ERROR, 2026-08-06 — I RAN qa-gate.sh approve ON THIS TASK MYSELF, MID-IMPLEMENTATION.

I wanted the error_key that a no-completion-record approve produces, and instead of building a fixture I invoked the live gate:

  bash .claude/scripts/qa-gate.sh approve claude-workflow-plugin-qbhw 'probe: expect refusal'
  -> {"ok":false,...,"error_key":"impact_report_stale",...}

It refused, on a stale impact report, so no label was written and no record was created. But the refusal I got was incidental. Had the impact report been fresh and a completion record existed, THAT COMMAND WOULD HAVE APPROVED MY OWN DELEGATED WORK — the orchestrator signing off on a specialist's change set with no independent review. That is the single boundary the whole workflow exists to enforce, and CLAUDE.md's first rule is that the orchestrator does not do the specialists' work; approving is further over the line than editing.

WHAT MADE IT EASY TO DO: I was diagnosing, not approving, and the command that answers a diagnostic question happens to be the command that performs the irreversible action. There is no read-only 'what would approve say' mode. The correct move was a fixture — the component harness exists precisely so the gate can be driven without touching a live task.

WHY I AM RECORDING IT RATHER THAN MOVING ON: the gate stopped me for an unrelated reason. Treating 'it refused' as 'no harm done' would be reading a lucky outcome as a safe procedure, which is the exact shape this phase has documented twenty-four times. The next attempt on a task with a fresh report would not refuse.

WORTH CONSIDERING AS A FIX, not filed as one because it needs thought: approve has no --dry-run. Every other destructive path in this repo has one (worktree-sweep's default IS dry-run; beads-ledger reconcile requires --apply; qa-gate reconcile-tracker reports before writing). approve is the most consequential write in the system and the only way to ask it a question is to make it act.

R1-F1 (HIGH) — .claude/scripts/qa-gate.sh:4612-4620, cmd_completion_record: the bjx field_name guard validates a string it does not write.
fields_csv is built with jq join(","), then re-split on IFS="," and subjected to PATHNAME EXPANSION by the unquoted `for fname in $fields_csv`. assert_record_scalar therefore sees post-join/post-split/post-glob words; the record writes the original fields_csv. Two reproductions through the component harness:
  (1) COMMA — deterministic, no adversary, no special CWD. Payload key "a,b" -> ok=true, record reads fields=...,a,b. One key rendered as two. The helper header states the opposite: "The class has no space, no colon, no comma and no bracket, so nothing that passes can ... split the csv."
  (2) GLOB — CWD-DEPENDENT. Payload key "[c]lean1" with a file "clean1" in CWD -> ok=true and the record carries a bracket. The SAME payload in an empty CWD -> ok=false, field_name_invalid_chars. Same input, opposite verdict, decided by unrelated files in the working directory.
No second layer catches either: validate-completion never inspects key names, and line 4617 is the only field_name guard in the tree. shellcheck is silent on the pattern in isolation (rc=0, no suppression directive present) — your clean lint run is not evidence against this and this was not a knowing suppression. P7-4b passes because its shape ("evil at 1999: 0 file(s)") has neither a glob metachar nor a comma, i.e. it sits exactly outside the hole.
The task description makes this an explicit criterion: every interpolated scalar must match ^[A-Za-z0-9._+-]+$, over three families including every field name. Current downstream harm is bounded (nothing parses fields= today; role= is ordering-protected; a payload_sha= injection would need attacker-controlled filenames in CWD). That bounds the blast radius, not the defect — this is the grammar the v5 phase will extend with unit_id/green_before/green_after/design_hash.

    while IFS= read -r fname; do

Three facts compose: (a) the persisted payload is keyed on the TASK only, so a second completion-record overwrites the first on disk; (b) latest_completion_record is latest-wins; (c) qa.md section 10 — edited in this change — orders QA to record its OWN contract BEFORE calling approve ("the record must go FIRST"), and documents QA files_changed as usually []. <!-- BD-MCP-META: {"kind":"qa-note","source":"qa-agent","round":3,"stage":"pre-tier-code-review"} -->
## QA round 3 — assessment of the two repair attempts (pre-tier, code review only)

Recorded now rather than at verdict time because a connection failure killed the previous round mid-write and this assessment would have died with it. **Verdict still pending the full 44-spec tier** (`/tmp/p7bar3.log`); this is the reading half only.

### Repair 1 — `worktree-approval-resolution.sh` (R2-F1): reasoning is correct, including the subtle part

Seeds the completion record inside `approve_in` rather than bypassing with `--no-completion`, and the stated reason is the right one: sections 1.5/1.6/3.1 assert approve's **side effects** (tracker truncation, baseline refresh, cross-worktree release), and a bypass that short-circuited before those would leave the legs green while testing nothing.

The load-bearing detail is `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR="$root"`, and their justification checks out by construction: `PROJECT_DIR="${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-$(pwd)}"` and `QA_TRACKING_DIR="$PROJECT_DIR/.claude/.qa-tracking"` (qa-gate.sh:153-154). So seeding against the **primary** while approving in the **worktree** would have put the payload in a checkout the approve never reads — and their description of the resulting failure is precisely accurate: the record would still satisfy the refusal (records are bd comments, one shared database) while the completeness cross-check silently degraded to `unestablished`. That is a real trap, correctly identified, and it is exactly the kind that passes a green run.

Seeding through `"$qg"` (the same writer the leg approves with) is also right — a mutant copy is then exercised end-to-end. `$san` is in scope at the insertion point.

### Repair 2 — `gate-baseline-v2.sh` (R2-F2): this is the fix I would have specified, and it proves itself

I had written into R2-F2 that any loosening "must be paired with a leg proving the assertion STILL goes red when a real call survives the strip", because an over-loosened repair converts a loud-but-imprecise guard into a silent-and-vacuous one. The repair arrives at that independently and implements all three directions:

- **Sensitivity** — appends `reconcile_tracker || true` to a copy, asserts the anchor fires (1).
- **Specificity** — appends a comment naming the function, asserts it does not fire (0).
- **Control** — asserts the OLD bare-text anchor could not tell those two copies apart. Measured, not narrated.

`executable_refs` is sound: it asks about the **line's kind**, not the file's prose, so a line beginning with optional whitespace then `#` cannot contain a call in any shell. It is over-strict in one direction only (a trailing comment on a code line is still counted), which is the safe direction. Declining to write a `#`-stripping pass is the right call for the reason given — that means deciding whether a `#` sits inside a string, a `${var#pat}`, or a `$#`, i.e. parsing shell with a regex inside a checker whose job is to be more trustworthy than what it checks.

### On the framing that scoped this fix — I disagree, and the disagreement matters

The brief to the specialist was that `gbv2-7M` is *more serious* than the migration gap because "a guard in already-committed code is no longer proving what it claims." I reproduced it, and that is not what happened:

Running the spec's own strip against the shipped `qa-gate.sh`, **exactly one line survives, and it is a comment, not a call** — the header sentence in `completion_files_crosscheck` noting that the reconciler emits absolute paths (`git diff -U0` confirms it as a `+` line from P7). **No `reconcile_tracker` call survives the strip.** The property the guard asserts — that the mutant is a faithful pre-94d script rather than a broken one — held the entire time. Every downstream "with the reconcile stripped" leg was still measuring what it claimed.

The direction of failure is the safe one, and that is the whole distinction. `R1-F1` and `R1-F4` were HIGH precisely because each made a guard announce **success** over the exact input it existed to catch. `gbv2-7M` announced **failure** over an input that was fine. A false positive in a guard is noisy and must be fixed; a false negative is the catastrophic one. Ranking this above the migration gap inverts that ordering.

Why it mattered practically: "the guarantee was lost, restore it" scopes toward *make it green*, and the cheapest way to do that is to reword P7's comment so the grep stops matching — which would degrade a precise code comment to appease a test and leave the proxy just as brittle for the next prose mention (the spec's own header already anticipates such prose). The correct scoping is the one that landed: the assertion's proxy (text count) never matched its stated claim (call count), so re-cut the anchor to measure the claim and prove it both fires and does not false-fire.

So: **MEDIUM, not HIGH; disagree with the framing, agree with the fix** — which is better than the framing that produced it. `R2-F1` (the worktree migration gap) remains the only open finding at or above threshold, because that one is genuine coverage loss on a shipped production path.
