<!-- BD-MCP-META: {"kind":"implementation-note","source":"devops-agent","task":"claude-workflow-plugin-bjx"} -->
## bjx — reachability verdict, option chosen, and what the test pins

### 1. Reachability verdict: STILL REACHABLE at HEAD (37b4a1e). Outcome 1, with an outcome-3 twist.

Reproduced deterministically before touching anything, on real `bd` in a component fixture, with label state read from the **SQLite `labels` table** rather than `bd show` (l1r.3: WAL writes without an mtime bump make `bd show` unreliable for exactly this transition — DB and `bd show` agreed in every run here, but the reads were done both ways).

Four scenarios, pre-fix:

| # | Sequence | `enter` clears? | `approve` warns? |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | `enter` -> `grade-record(satisfied)` -> `approve` | no | no |
| R2 | `enter` -> `grade-record(satisfied)` -> **`enter`** -> `approve` | **YES** | **YES** |
| R3 | R2, with the `enter` **extracted from the live Stop block text** | **YES** | — |
| R4 | grade, then change set moves, then `enter` | YES | YES (correct here) |

**Your session observation was right, and so was the bug report.** R1 is the relay as practised — `enter` at task start, `grade-record`, `approve`, never re-entering — and it does not fire. Nothing in gz3 fixed this; gz3 touched `cmd_approve`'s idempotency guard and left the `cmd_enter` rubric block untouched.

**The twist that decided the fix: the ordering is not a prompt convention, it is printed by a hook.** The canonical RUBRIC-RELAY (orchestrator.md 5a) has no `enter` step at all — steps are A read cap/packet, B spawn grader, C `grade-record`, D re-spawn QA. `grade-record` therefore runs in the **orchestrator's** turn and QA acts on the verdict in a **later spawn**. Any Stop in between blocks, and the block text says:

```
When entering review, mark the gate:
  bash .claude/scripts/qa-gate.sh enter $TASK_ID
```

(`verify-before-stop.sh`; the `LABEL_WITHOUT_RECORD` remediation prints the same `enter` as step 1 of its 3-command recipe.) In R3 I extracted that exact line from the live `.reason` and ran it verbatim: `rubric-satisfied` present, change set **provably unmoved** (`8685efdc…` before and after), and the verdict was destroyed. So the reported ordering is one the relay reaches **by construction**, on an instruction the gate authors itself.

**Severity, corrected upward from "friction".** `approve` then emits `WARNING approving with rubric-pending still set (no satisfied verdict on file)` — factually false, with the satisfied `RUBRIC` comment for the identical hash still on the task — and `qa.md` 6f answers that warning with a mandatory written **OVERRIDE reason**. So the gate was manufacturing override records against its own audit trail (RELEASE_AUDIT R9's "every approval cites a verdict or an override" quietly degrades), or driving a second paid grader spawn for an already-graded diff.

### 2. Mechanism at pre-fix line numbers

- `qa-gate.sh:796-805` — `cmd_enter` reads `rubric-satisfied` and calls `remove_rubric_satisfied` **unconditionally**.
- `qa-gate.sh:814` — the idempotent re-enter branch re-adds `rubric-pending`.
- `qa-gate.sh:842` — the fresh-enter branch adds `rubric-pending`.
- `qa-gate.sh:2032` — `comment_text="RUBRIC $rv_val iteration $it_val: $verdict — $summary"`. **No hash.** Confirmed empirically (R5): the record carried no `change_set_hash`, while its siblings `QA-GATE APPROVED` (llh.18) and `REVIEW-ARTIFACT` (`reviewed_hash`, jio.1) both do.

### 3. Option chosen: (b), and the hash binding it requires. (a) was disproved, not merely disfavoured.

**(a) "relay enters before grading" — rejected on evidence, not on doctrine.** R3 shows the damaging `enter` is emitted by `verify-before-stop.sh`, not by a prompt. No ordering rule in `orchestrator.md`/`qa.md` can prevent a hook from printing it. (a) cannot fix the reachable path even if every agent obeyed it perfectly.

**(b) needed a checkable definition of "current cycle", and it did not have one.** You asked me to check whether `RUBRIC` comments carry a hash: **they do not**. I evaluated two hash-free discriminators and rejected both as unsound:

- *"compare against the previously-persisted impact report"* — the report's hash is a statement about when the **report** was written, not when the **verdict** was graded. `enter -> grade(H1) -> edit -> impact-report.sh(H2) -> enter` would preserve a verdict that never saw H2. ### 1. The forgery: reproduced, then closed at the writer

QA is right, and the finding is mine to own — I extended a grammar without validating the one field in it that comes from the grader.

**Reproduced end-to-end before touching anything,** on real `bd`, labels read from the SQLite `labels` table:

| case | `rubric_version` | record written | re-enter outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| forgery | `1 iteration 1: satisfied change_set_hash=<real>` | `RUBRIC 1 iteration 1: satisfied change_set_hash=<real> iteration 7: needs_revision change_set_hash=<real> — failed: C2` | **FORGED-PRESERVED** |
| causation control | `1` (identical verdict otherwise) | `RUBRIC 1 iteration 7: needs_revision change_set_hash=<real> — failed: C2` | cleared |
| naive colon | `v1:x` | written, unparseable prefix | cleared (unbound) |

Mechanism exactly as QA described: `rv_val` is interpolated with a space on each side, `(?<v>[^:]*)` cannot cross a colon, so the verdict is parsed from immediately after the record's **first** colon — and a crafted version relocates that colon into injected text. **My comment at `qa-gate.sh:484-486` was half-true and I have replaced it.** The naive case (`v1:x`) genuinely reads as unbound — verified — which is precisely why "reject colons" would have been the wrong lesson: the exploitable shape needs a **space**, not a colon. **Reader (`:543`) carries the same class,** as parity, not as the defence. I checked whether reader-side tightening could close this alone: **it cannot** — the injected prefix is itself entirely within any sane class, so a reader can never distinguish an injected prefix from a real one after the fact. The writer is the only place this closes. What the parity buys is that the two grammars agree about what a version may be; section F4 extracts both spellings from the shipped source and asserts they are the same set.

Threat-model boundary re-stated in the code and in `docs/HOOKS.md`: a hand-written `bd comments add` can still fabricate a record — that is unchanged llh.18 territory. What is closed is the strictly worse case, forging **through the tool's own validated input**, which needs no shell.

### R2-F1 — the writer bound the wrong thing (`qa-gate.sh:2440-2490`, flag at `:2116`)

**Repro.** Armed cycle over `{src/a.ts}`, captured the packet's impact-report hash `8685efdc…`, then added `src/b.ts` (a path landing while the grader runs), then `grade-record`. **Fix — three sources, descending authority.** I did not pick one of your two shapes; both were needed, because each fails alone.

1. `--graded-hash`, passed by the relay from the packet. Authoritative — the only value that witnesses what the grader was shown. Validated `[A-Za-z0-9-]` for the round-2 reason: it is operator input going into the machine prefix. **Not** taken from the grader's JSON — that would let the graded party state what it graded, and would change `grader.md`'s schema.
2. Live recompute **corroborated by the persisted impact report**. You were right that the report can move — so it is used as a *witness*, not a source: if it still describes the current set, nothing was added since the packet was built. This is what keeps the flag optional without making the fallback a lie.
3. Neither → record **UNBOUND**, naming both hashes. Unbound is not a failure mode: `enter` treats it as stale and clears, i.e. pre-bjx behaviour, and the next relay round re-grades.

**Residual, stated rather than hidden:** if the report is itself regenerated after packet assembly (an `enter` between steps C and D does exactly that), it agrees with live while describing a set the grader never saw. Only the flag closes that, which is why the relay now passes it — and why F2's cross-check is the backstop.

**Repro + control.** `satisfied@1` then `needs_revision@1.5` → the stale satisfied hash survived re-entry; the integer control (`needs_revision@2`) cleared. Only the iteration format differed.

**Which half is load-bearing: the READER.** Verified, not assumed, and the verification is the interesting part:

- A superseding record written **by hand** (legacy build, paste, another tool) reproduces the bug on the shipped script. No writer validation can reach it. So the writer half cannot be sufficient.
- Differential at the reader level, on the same input: pre-fix program → `abc123` (resurrects the superseded hash), shipped program → empty. End-to-end with only the selector differing: `PRESERVED` vs `cleared`.

So J3 is a **differential** (extract the shipped expression, compare against the literal pre-fix expression on one input, assert they disagree) rather than a script mutation: if either program breaks, the disagreement assertion catches it. A control on an input with no unparseable record asserts the two otherwise agree.

- Regional/transient model exclusions in .claude/model-ranking go stale silently: a `!family` line added for a temporary outage keeps masking downstream behavior (here it collapsed the v4 top==opus-class role split onto Opus for six weeks) long after the outage clears. Gate every un-exclusion on FRESH spawn evidence (subagent-spawns.log + effort-ab logs naming the model), not memory, and date the rationale + rollback line in the file. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-bi3.2 --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-25 -->
- Files rewritten by a helper (awk/mv, e.g. workflow-model-apply.sh) instead of the Edit/Write tool never land in changed-files.txt, so the QA impact hash and the change-set-bound approval only cover Edit-tracked files. When a task mutates files via a helper, QA must verify those files explicitly via git diff (not rely on the impact report alone). <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-bi3.2 --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-25 -->
- MCP registration scope is a mechanical contract, not etiquette: a detection probe reads ONE config path (top-level .mcpServers of ~/.claude.json for user scope), so local/project-scope registrations are silently invisible — verify the probe read path when writing setup docs and make wrong-scope the first troubleshooting row. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-1vq.2 --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-25 -->
- Published CLI config references can lag the shipped binary: verify accepted values against the binary own introspection surface (e.g. codex debug models) rather than the docs or trial-and-error, and record the lag in the operator doc so editors re-verify. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-1vq.2 --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-25 -->
- Run suites via their canonical make targets: a bare runner invocation (npx vitest run) includes guarded paid live specs whose fail-closed API-key errors masquerade as regressions; the CI-shaped target (make test-e2e-unit) is the comparable baseline. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-1vq.2 --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-25 -->
- When a change adds a second independent gate to a release path, every META that isolates the FIRST gate must be re-seeded to satisfy the new gate so it still fails for its own reason (jio.1 MM18 migration is the template). <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-jio.1 --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-26 -->
- A deliberate second implementation of a gate predicate (shell counter + TS live invariant) is only a second witness if QA diffs the two rule-by-rule against the writer grammars at their emit sites — the jio.2 parity review caught a greedy-sed vs first-match token-selection divergence (gqp) that every test suite had missed. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-jio.2 --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-26 -->
- Trace-anchor refreshes that add a skip must be legitimized against the on-disk cassette (jq has(field) on the replay file), not the spec comment — and the pin must assert skipped+pass+exact detail so a future re-record flips loud instead of silently inheriting the skip. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-jio.2 --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-26 -->
- State a gate writes for its own bookkeeping can destroy the evidence a later check needs: qa-gate.sh approve truncates changed-files.txt, so re-running impact-report.sh --hash-only in the approving checkout returns the empty-list hash and can never reproduce the approved hash — even there. Any cross-checkout or after-the-fact verification must read the PERSISTED record (impact-report-<tid>.json, which survives approve), never recompute; assert the destruction in the test so making it conditional fails loudly instead of silently disabling the reader. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-3mg.2 --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-26 -->
- The two-file awk join idiom NR==FNR is true for every record of the SECOND file when the first file contributes zero records — an empty first input silently swallows the entire join; load the lookup file in BEGIN via getline and add a structural row-count self-check instead. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-gzc --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-26 -->
- jq empty is not a merge-input validity oracle — it accepts empty files and multi-document streams; any jq -s merge that indexes .[0]/.[1] positionally must gate its inputs on "length == 1 and (.[0] | type == \"object\")" or the second document of a corrupted input silently binds as the other merge side. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-p5n --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-26 -->
- Add-if-absent config clauses must key on presence (has("key")), never value truthiness — an operator-owned key holding an explicit null or false is still operator-owned, and truthiness guards silently clobber it on upgrade. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-p5n --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-26 -->
- When a reviewer finding names one call site, sweep every sibling call site with the same shape before resolving — the p5n settings merge carried the identical positional-binding hole the finding named for .mcp.json, and the sweep (J27 step 6) is what made the resolution complete rather than symptomatic. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-p5n --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-26 -->
- When adding a new rung to a detection ladder, probe every input class the EARLIER rungs already claim — an earlier detector can shadow the new rung for inputs its comment says it covers (v2 signal 2 vs detect_v3 signal (b) on deleted-manifest trees), leaving documented coverage dead on arrival. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-x15 --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-27 -->
- install.sh run from outside a checkout-shaped directory silently clones the plugin source from the network — any A/B comparison of installer versions (probes, METAs, specs) must run each version from a local git-archive tree, never from an extracted single file. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-pnf --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-27 -->
- An invariant that is only nearly true — a probe reporting "no file changes" while one file is written — is one a future change can break without failing a test. Count the write or delete the claim. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-56r --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-27 -->
- A path-traversal guard written as a string test on the path is not a containment guard: [ -f ] and hashing both follow symlinks, so the only sound checks are physical containment of the resolved path, or refusing path shapes the producer never emits (e.g. root scope is flat by construction). <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-56r --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-27 -->
- A brace group composed with `{ ... } > file || fail-arm` must not end on a guarded command like `[ -n "$x" ] && printf` — the guard rc becomes the group rc on the empty case and fires the failure arm after every write succeeded; end such groups with an unconditional command (e.g. `:` or an always-true printf). <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-n64 --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-27 -->
- A BOM-less .ps1 is decoded as ANSI by Windows PowerShell 5.1, and non-ASCII bytes inside string literals can decode to smart quotes (U+201D/U+201E terminate double-quoted strings per the PS grammar) — keep PowerShell source ASCII outside whole-line comments, guard it mechanically, and compose any required non-ASCII output at runtime via [char]0xNNNN. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-m7e --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-27 -->
- When a source literal must change encoding but its rendered output is byte-pinned to another implementation, compose the character at runtime and make the parity extractor resolve the composition — then guard both directions (a literal-reintroduction check AND a wrong-codepoint check) so neither the source property nor the output parity can silently regress. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-m7e --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-27 -->
- When a change extends an installer copy surface into an operator-owned directory, every preservation leg must be extended in the same change — upgrade backup, update backup, fresh-path guard, and uninstall — and the regression test must assert the backup CONTAINS the replaced bytes, not that the report says so. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-36z --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-27 -->
- When summarizing a JSON artifact, prove the jq path resolves before reporting a count: jq length of null is 0, so a wrong path yields a confident zero with no error rather than a failure. Per-file impact-report entries store the raw MCP envelope, so the payload is at .impact.data.nodes, not .impact.nodes. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-gz3 --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-27 -->
- Agent Bash tooling here runs under zsh, which does not word-split unquoted expansions: `git diff -- $FILES` passes one newline-joined pathspec that matches nothing and silently yields an empty diff. Build multi-path command arguments as arrays and verify the output names every expected file. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-gz3 --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-27 -->
- A reviewer own claims are the ones least likely to be checked, because the checking machinery is pointed outward: on gl6 the same agent named "measure, do not assert" as the cycle recurring defect class and then asserted an untested provenance claim in four consecutive rounds, and one round after naming "enumerate the full state space of what you guard" proposed a guard covering one operand of a two-operand comparison. Naming a review heuristic does not internalise it — apply it to your own output first. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-gl6 --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-28 -->
- A validation built from the same operation as the mutation cannot see that operation own distortion: filtering both sides of a comparison with the identical grep makes a broken or over-broad filter compare equal to itself and report success. Use an independent oracle (the real parser, not a mirror of the edit), and test an oracle by BREAKING the thing it observes — a mirror is indistinguishable from an independent check while the filter still works. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-gl6 --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-28 -->
- Do not infer success from empty output: propagate the exit status of what you actually ran. A comparison that never happened prints nothing, which is the same observable as a comparison that found nothing — nine of fourteen operand states made diff exit 2 with empty stdout while a file-type guard on one operand stayed silent. Branch on rc, not on silence, and prefer one status check over a taxonomy of file-type tests. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-gl6 --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-28 -->

Automation there is on a decay clock regardless of how carefully written, so weigh whether the convenience is worth a permanently unverifiable surface: on gl6 a 103-line sweep that saved a one-line hand edit produced eleven of thirteen findings, and a hand edit verified by the real parser has none of them. <!-- sources: claude-workflow-plugin-gl6 --> <!-- recorded: 2026-07-28 -->

# Default rubric (v1)

Applies to every task graded under the rubric-grader QA loop (spec Phase A). Each criterion below is a pass/fail assertion the grader evaluates from the grading packet: `bd show` for the task, the SPEC doc, the diff of the files listed in `.qa-tracking/changed-files.txt`, the F7 completion contract returned by the specialist, and `LESSONS.md`. One-line justification per criterion. No numeric score theater — pass or fail.

The criteria are intentionally short and checkable. Where the criterion needs context (boundary-mock fidelity, F7 fields), the "Evidence that satisfies it" line names the artefact the grader looks at.

## Criteria

### C1. Behavior matches the task description and SPEC.

The shipped diff implements the behavior the task description asks for, and matches the goal + acceptance criteria stated in the attached SPEC doc (read via `bd_doc_read(task_id, name="spec")`). Out-of-scope behavior the SPEC explicitly excludes is NOT in the diff.

Evidence that satisfies it: a 1-2 sentence walk-through that maps every user-visible behavior in the SPEC to a code path in the diff (or to a deliberate, documented deferral in the F7 `decisions` array). A diff that adds plausibly-related behavior the SPEC does not name fails this criterion — that is scope creep.

### C2. Tests added exercise user behavior rather than implementation.

Where the diff introduces new behavior, the diff also introduces tests that assert against the user-visible contract (return shape, side effects, error envelope, accessibility role, status code) rather than against the implementation's private structure (function-name mocking, line-coverage gymnastics, internal control-flow assertions).

Evidence that satisfies it: at least one test in the diff that would still pass if the implementation were rewritten while keeping the user contract identical. A test that asserts only against private symbols, internal call counts, or framework boilerplate fails this criterion.

### C3. The F7 completion contract carries all six fields with substantive `llm_observations`.

The specialist's structured completion payload includes `task_id`, `files_changed`, `tests_added`, `decisions`, `blockers`, and `llm_observations`. `llm_observations` is non-trivial narrative — what surprised the specialist, what was unclear, what they noticed and did not act on. A boilerplate one-liner like "no observations" fails this criterion (principle 9: `llm_observations` is mandatory and substantive).

Evidence that satisfies it: each of the six fields is present and the `llm_observations` paragraph is the kind of thing a human engineer would say at a stand-up.

### C4. No unrelated scope in the diff.

Every file the specialist touched serves the task. Drive-by refactors, formatting churn on untouched lines, and "while I'm here" cleanups that exceed the task brief fail this criterion — they should be filed as paired follow-up Beads tasks instead.

Evidence that satisfies it: the diff's file list maps cleanly to the SPEC's deliverables; any incidental change is either trivial (one-line typo fix) or explicitly justified in the `decisions` array.

### C5. J26 modules relevant to the diff are addressed.

Where the diff touches a domain covered by the J26 security taxonomy (SECRETS, INJECTION, AUTH, CONFIG, DEPS, AI, MOBILE, DATA — see `docs/AGENTS.md`), the diff demonstrates that the relevant modules were considered. Untouched J26 domains are out of scope.

Evidence that satisfies it: the `decisions` array (or the SPEC) names which J26 modules apply, and the diff shows defences in those modules (input validation at the trust boundary, parameterised queries, narrow CORS, audited logging, etc.). A diff that touches user input handling without naming INJECTION fails this criterion.

### C6. Docs updated where behavior changed.

When the diff changes user-visible behavior, the documentation that describes that behavior is updated in the same change. This includes `CHANGELOG.md`, README sections, `docs/*.md`, command help text, and SPEC docs the diff renders out of date.

Evidence that satisfies it: a docs-only file in `files_changed` paired with each behavioral change, or a deliberate `decisions` entry stating why a doc deferral is correct (e.g. an internal refactor that ships without user-visible change). A behavioral change that ships with no doc update and no deferral note fails this criterion.

### C7. Boundary-mock fidelity (LESSONS.md lesson 2).

When the diff introduces or modifies mocks of boundaries the project does not control (third-party HTTP APIs, external SDKs, system calls, message-bus payloads), every such mock derives its shape from a fixture extracted from the real downstream producer's spec (OpenAPI, proto file, SDK source, vendor docs). The fixture's source is cited in a comment, the `decisions` array, or `llm_observations`.

**Automatic needs_revision:** circular pass-through assertions are an immediate fail. A mock that feeds `body.error` so a test can assert `body.error` proves nothing — it tests the test's own setup, not the production behavior. Cite `LESSONS.md` lesson 2 in the justification.

Evidence that satisfies it: every new boundary mock points at a fixture file (`.fixtures/`, `__fixtures__/`, `testdata/`) carrying a snapshot of the producer's payload, and the fixture has a comment naming the source (URL, commit, SDK version). Tests assert against the producer's contract, not against the mock's own input.

# DevOps rubric (v1)

Applied additionally when the task carries the `devops` label. Default criteria still apply; these add domain-specific checks pulled from `.claude/agents/devops.md`. The leverage is default + bugfix — these are the few devops-specific failure modes that recur.

## Criteria

### D1. Scripts are idempotent and re-runnable.

Install, uninstall, hook, and CI scripts in the diff produce the same end state when run twice in a row. A second run of `install.sh` does not double-write hooks, clobber prior settings, or fail because a directory already exists. A migration script that exits non-zero on its second run fails this criterion.

Evidence that satisfies it: every new script uses `mkdir -p`, conditional inserts, and idempotent label operations (`bd label add` returns success if already present); the `decisions` array documents any deliberately non-idempotent step (e.g. a one-shot data migration) and pairs it with a guard (lock file, completion sentinel) so a re-run is detected.

### D2. Graceful degradation on missing optional tools.

When the diff depends on an optional tool (gitleaks, shellcheck, a particular bd version, a specific CI runner image), the missing-tool path is handled: log a structured warning, fall back to a safe default, exit zero where the workflow allows. A hook that exits non-zero because `gitleaks` is not installed fails this criterion — that is not a developer-machine-portable failure mode.

Evidence that satisfies it: every new tool dependency is probed (`command -v tool >/dev/null`); the fallback path is documented in the script comments and tested at L1; the `decisions` array names the dependency and its installation hint.

### D3. No new permission prompts; autonomy preserved.

The diff does not add `permissions.deny` rules to `settings.json`, narrow specialist tool lists below the broad allow set, or introduce any user-facing approval step the plugin previously ran without. Principle 3 of the v3 plan is "full autonomy, no permission prompts" — every deny rule becomes a future approval prompt and breaks the workflow.

Evidence that satisfies it: a diff of `.claude/settings.json` shows only `permissions.allow` expansions, never `deny`; specialist tool frontmatter is unchanged or expanded; the `decisions` array calls out any new tool the broadened allow set covers.

### D4. Secrets and PII stay out of source, logs, and history.

Hardcoded API keys, tokens, passwords, private keys, committer emails, and PII are absent from the diff. Logs that the diff adds redact sensitive fields before writing. A commit that introduces an `.env` file with values, a personal email address in a script header, or unredacted PII in a log line fails this criterion (extends C5 / SECRETS + DATA).

Evidence that satisfies it: secrets read from a secret manager or environment variable at runtime; PII fields in new log lines are redacted (`***@`, `user_id=***`); a `gitleaks`-equivalent pass on the diff is clean, and the `decisions` array names the secrets the diff touches.

# Bugfix overlay (v1)

Applied additionally whenever the task type is `bug` (created with `-t bug` or carrying the `bug` label). Default + the relevant domain rubric still apply; this overlay enforces the evidence-before-fix protocol from spec 0.5. The protocol exists to break symptom-patching chains — speculative fixes stacking into double-digit follow-up PRs for a single issue, none of which can be proved to be the one that worked. Every criterion below is mandatory for bug-typed tasks.

## Criteria

### G1. A failing test demonstrating the root cause exists and predates the fix.

The diff contains a test that fails on the broken commit and passes on the fix commit. The test is committed BEFORE the fix in the commit sequence (or in a single commit if the workflow squashes), so a reviewer can run the test against the parent of the fix and watch it fail.

Evidence that satisfies it: the commit log (or the diff structure) shows the test arriving before the fix; the test is keyed to the user-visible symptom in the bug report, not to an internal symptom the fix happens to flip. A diff where the test and the fix arrive in the same blob with no failing-test evidence fails this criterion. A test that asserts only against the fix's new code path (and would not have been red against the broken version) also fails — it does not demonstrate the root cause.

### G2. A root-cause statement with cited evidence is attached to the Beads task.

The Beads task carries a comment in the shape "X did Y because W; evidence: Z" — with actual evidence: a trace excerpt, a `git bisect` SHA, log lines, a profiler output, a network HAR. A prose hand-wave without a citation fails this criterion. The evidence must name the specific input, code path, or contract that flips behavior.

Evidence that satisfies it: a Beads comment (or a section in `notes`) on the task that cites at least one concrete artefact — file:line of the bad code, a deploy log timestamp, a database row that triggered the failure. "Probably a race condition" with no trace fails.

### G3. The fix rationale contains no speculative language.

The `decisions` array, `llm_observations`, and the Beads notes describe the fix in declarative terms: "the X path now does Y; this makes Z hold because W". Hedging language — "might", "should fix", "probably", "in theory", "I think this works" — fails this criterion. Speculation in the fix description is the strongest signal that the root cause is not understood and the patch is a guess.

Evidence that satisfies it: a reviewer can read the fix rationale and predict, without running the test, whether the patch addresses the documented root cause. If the rationale leaves the reviewer guessing, this criterion fails.

### G4. The fix flips the failing test from G1.

The test added in G1 fails on the pre-fix code and passes on the post-fix code — exactly. A test that was already passing before the fix and continues to pass is not regression coverage; it is a smoke check. The fix must be the change that turns the test from red to green.

Evidence that satisfies it: a side-by-side run against the parent commit and the fix commit shows the same test transitioning from FAIL to PASS. If the test passes on both sides, G4 fails (and likely G1 fails too — the test does not encode the root cause).

Approved on the change set the grader was shown: change_set_hash=1ddfecdc5c6a893a83801d5f4578fcffe292c8f80f3b2b346a035d6f9b4c3121, verified identical across the live tracker, the persisted impact report, the RUBRIC record, and the review artifact reviewed_hash.

THE FIXS OWN RELAY PATH AUTHORISED IT. The grading that produced this verdict exercised R2-F1s fix and took the authoritative branch: the packet header hash was passed verbatim as --graded-hash and the relay reported "source: --graded-hash supplied by the relay". I verified the packet header hash equals the recorded hash. Precision note: in this state live == packet, so the durable record alone cannot discriminate source 1 from source 2 — the branch is attested by the relay envelope, not re-derived by me.

WHAT WAS FIXED, AND WHY THE OTHER OPTION WAS DISPROVED RATHER THAN DISFAVOURED. cmd_enter cleared rubric-satisfied unconditionally, destroying verdicts recorded seconds earlier against the identical change set, after which approve warned "no satisfied verdict on file" — false, with the proving RUBRIC comment on the same task — and qa.md 6f answers that warning with a mandatory written OVERRIDE reason. The gate was manufacturing overrides against its own audit trail and driving paid re-grades. The alternative fix (make the relay enter before grading) is not merely worse, it is unsound: the damaging enter is PRINTED BY THE HOOK, at verify-before-stop.sh:1977 (QA-required block) and :1801 (LABEL_WITHOUT_RECORD remediation), both of which I confirmed at the line, as did the grader independently. No ordering rule in any prompt can stop a hook from printing a command. Section D drives the command extracted from the live block text, so the disproof is pinned rather than argued.

SIX DEFECTS ACROSS THREE REVIEW ROUNDS — ALL SIX IN THE NEW MACHINERY, NONE IN THE ORIGINAL BUG. The reported bug was label friction. The machinery introduced to fix it correctly (a hash-bound record grammar plus a conditional preservation guard) generated: (1) a grammar injection via unvalidated rubric_version, which relocated the records first colon so a needs_revision verdict read back as satisfied AND bound — closed at the writer with ^[A-Za-z0-9._+-]+$; (2) the path-scoped binding limit — pinned as documented behaviour in section B3 and corrected in all four prose sites, NOT narrowed, because the hash is the single canonicalisation shared with the qa-approved record (llh.18) and reviewed_hash (jio.1) and a content hash inside cmd_enter would be the fourth definition llh.18 forbids; (3) the sha256-unavailable sentinel, a non-empty CONSTANT that compared equal to itself and so fired preservation unconditionally on a host with no sha tool — refused in three places behind one named symbol, and I verified end to end that such a host CLEARS rather than wedges and that approve still releases; (4-6) Sols three HIGHs below.

SOLS THREE HIGH FINDINGS AT ITERATION 2 — its third success in twelve attempts, and the third time it found what the Claude lane had cleared. R2-F1: the writer bound the LIVE tracker at record time rather than what was graded, a PATH leak distinct from the content-only limit. Fixed with three sources in descending authority, all three verified by me: the flag binds the packet hash even when live has moved; no-flag binds only when the persisted report corroborates it; neither leaves the record UNBOUND naming both hashes. A crafted --graded-hash is refused with graded_hash_invalid_chars, exit 1, nothing recorded. Reading the hash from the graders JSON was correctly rejected — the grader is both the judging party and one whose output is shaped by the diff it reads, so that would be the rubric_version injection with extra steps. R2-F2: approve claimed the verdict from the LABEL alone. R2-F3: a superseded verdict survived by being unparseable.

F3s GAP PROVED BROADER THAN THE SINGLE SHAPE SOL REPORTED. Differentialling the round-2 reader against the round-3 reader, ANY unreadable latest record resurrected the older verdict — four shapes verified (bad version, non-integer iteration, a bare RUBRIC line, and plain prose beginning RUBRIC ), not just the reported one. The load-bearing half is the reader (select the latest record, then parse it); no writer validation can reach a hand-written record, which I reproduced. Anti-overreach holds: a comment not starting with RUBRIC does not displace a verdict.

THE F1 RESIDUAL IS STATED OPENLY, NOT HIDDEN, AND I VERIFIED IT IS REAL AND BOUNDED. A report regenerated after packet assembly agrees with live while describing an ungraded set, and the envelope still claims corroboration; only --graded-hash closes it, which I confirmed on byte-identical state. F2 is the backstop, which is why the residual is acceptable rather than merely disclosed.

WARN-NOT-REFUSE ON F2 IS CORRECT, AND I JUDGED IT AS THE ROLE PRINCIPLE 6 IS ABOUT. qa.md 6f already states that script-side rubric denial "would create a parallel gate and violate principle 6"; verify-before-stop.sh reads ZERO rubric state (0 matches, re-confirmed at approve time, and corroborated independently by the grader), so a script-side refusal would build an asymmetric half-gate that blocks at approve while Stop ignores it. The decisive argument is the exit test: every review-check.sh refusal has a legitimate free exit (author an artifact, change reviewer, resolve-finding or arbitrate), whereas a rubric refusal has none — a paid re-grade impossible at cap, or the label-removal dead end gz3 spent a task eliminating. A refusal whose only exit is a bypass teaches the bypass. So the distinction is principled, not special pleading. The harm was the audit trail lying, and that is fixed: three hash-checked states, with a mismatch visible BOTH in the approve envelope at decision time and in this durable record as [rubric mismatch: graded=<h> approved=<h>]. L3 pins the non-refusal so any reversal must argue with principle 6 at that line.

A FIXTURE HAD BEEN ENCODING THE BUG. Five existing assertions broke and all five were true signals. The most instructive: B2s fixture relied on the writer recomputing the live tracker — that reliance WAS R2-F1, so the test was encoding the defect. And I6s sentinel stub never wrote a report, so post-F1 every record was unbound for the CORROBORATION reason rather than the sentinel one, silently robbing that META of its attribution. I verified both re-baselines are corrections and not accommodations by re-running the whole spec on a pristine pre-fix worktree: B2 and I6 are STILL RED there. B2 does not discriminate F1, but section K does (K1/K2/K4 all RED pre-fix), which is correct decomposition rather than masking.

THREE METHODOLOGY NEAR-MISSES, ONE CLASS. Round 2: a bash-only mutation missed a guard living inside the jq program. Round 3: two attempts at a mutated reader produced a jq program that ERRORED, and an erroring reader answers empty — indistinguishable from the fix working. Plus I6s stub. All the same shape: an ABSENCE passing for the intended reason when it occurred for an unrelated one. The response was right — J3 is a differential with a control rather than a mutation — and I verified the control genuinely discriminates by running two deliberately broken programs through it: the disagree-on-input assertion alone passes for both, and the control catches both.

MY OWN TWO DISCLOSURES, recorded because they are the most useful thing here for the next reviewer. (1) FRAMING LOCK-IN: I tested the iteration field in round 2 across five hostile values and correctly found each reads unbound alone — but I framed it as an injection vector ("can this forge a binding?"), got a safe answer, and closed the line. F3 asks the opposite direction ("can this make a record unreadable, and what does that do to supersession?"). Same input, different question; a safe answer closes an input, not a field. That is why a second model caught it, and a deliberately re-framed second pass would have too. (2) I SHOULD HAVE FOUND qa.md 6f MYSELF in round 2 — I reviewed the approve/rubric interaction without citing the document that governs whether the script may refuse, and the implementer found it. Both are proposed as LESSONS.md entries.

EVIDENCE. Spec arc 68 -> 107 -> 149 assertions, sections A-L with 4 METAs; RED 86 pass / 63 fail on my own pristine worktree at 37b4a1e -> GREEN 149/149, with every acceptance assertion red pre-fix and every must-not-regress one already green. L1 26/26. L2 38/38 at 1716 assertions. make lint exit 0; the new spec shellchecked separately (claude-workflow-plugin-1z6: the canonical target does not cover component specs). manifest-validate OK. All 7 e2e fixture copies byte-identical by cmp. review-check.sh gate: independent, reviewer=sol-codex, 0 open findings, reviewed_hash matching. All five resolve-finding fix refs land exactly where claimed (:2116, :1391, :1622, :565, :2310), and the graders three independently-verified refs (verify-before-stop.sh:1801, :1977, impact-report.sh:283) are accurate.

RESIDUALS, all documented and none blocking: a hand-written bd comments add record can still fabricate a verdict (unchanged llh.18 threat boundary — what is closed is forging through the tools own validated input); the rubric paths refuse the sentinel while approve, Stop and review-check still accept it (impact-report.sh degraded mode, filed system-wide as claude-workflow-plugin-xii); the path-scoped limit; and a prose comment beginning with the literal RUBRIC clears a verdict, which is friction in the safe direction. Not done and flagged for the release: no CHANGELOG entry, no 4.1 section — a release decision at closeout.

## QA APPROVED — bjx. Post-approve verification and two disclosures.

**Approval is bound**: `change_set_hash=1ddfecdc…`, verified identical across the live tracker,
the persisted impact report, the RUBRIC record, and the review artifact's `reviewed_hash`
before I called approve. Final labels: `devops, qa-approved, rubric-satisfied`. Gate status
`approved`. `current-task` and the iteration counter cleared (F3/F4 side effects confirmed).

**F2's positive-verification state fired**, which is the outcome that matters most here — the
approve envelope reports `rubric-satisfied preserved (audit trail) and VERIFIED against this
approval — the satisfied verdict binds the same change set`, and the durable record carries
**no** mismatch token. So the machinery Sol's R2-F2 finding produced was exercised in its
agreeing branch by the very approval that ships it.

**One thing worth flagging for whoever audits this record.** My approval summary *quotes* the
mismatch token's spelling (`[rubric mismatch: graded=<h> approved=<h>]`) while explaining the
F2 mechanism, and my own first grep for the token consequently returned 1 — a false positive
against my own prose. There is **no genuine token**: an anchored search for real 64-hex hashes
returns nothing. I checked, and nothing outside `qa-gate.sh` parses that token (it is written
at :1622 and mentioned at :1396, never read), so this is harmless today. But it is the same
hazard class the anchored RUBRIC reader was hardened against in round 1, and the approval
record's suffix is *not* anchored — if a future auditing tool greps for `[rubric mismatch:`,
a summary that discusses the mechanism will trip it. Cheap mitigation if that ever ships:
match `graded=[0-9a-f]{40,}`, not the bare prefix.

### My two disclosures (recorded because they are the most transferable thing in this trail)

**1. Framing lock-in.** In round 2 I tested the `iteration` field across five hostile values
and correctly found each reads unbound *alone*. I framed the field as an **injection** vector
— "can this forge a binding?" — got a safe answer, and closed the line. R2-F3 asks the
opposite direction: "can this make a record *unreadable*, and what does that do to
supersession?" Same input, different question. A safe answer closes an **input**, not a
**field**. That is the real reason a second model caught it; a deliberately re-framed second
pass by the same model would have too.

**2. I should have found `qa.md` 6f myself.** In round 2 I reviewed the approve/rubric
interaction and formed a view on whether the script should refuse, without citing the
document that *governs* whether the script may refuse. The implementer found it and it
decided the question. Reviewing a policy boundary without reading the policy is the error.

### Candidate lessons — PROPOSED, not applied

Per qa.md section 9 I do not merge these; the orchestrator does.

```bash
bash .claude/scripts/lessons.sh add \
  'When probing a field for one threat direction, enumerate the others before closing it: a safe answer to "can this input forge X?" says nothing about "can this input make X unreadable?".' \
  --source claude-workflow-plugin-bjx

bash .claude/scripts/lessons.sh add \
  'A test whose acceptance is an ABSENCE (empty answer, cleared label, no binding) needs a control that discriminates the cause, not a stronger assertion — a broken or erroring implementation produces the same absence as a working one.' \
  --source claude-workflow-plugin-bjx
```

### Open, and deliberately not blocking
- Hand-written `bd comments add` record forgery — unchanged llh.18 threat boundary.
- Rubric-vs-approve sentinel asymmetry — `claude-workflow-plugin-xii`.
- Path-scoped binding limit — pinned by section B3, prose corrected in all four sites.
- A prose comment beginning with the literal `RUBRIC ` clears a verdict — friction in the safe direction.
- `claude-workflow-plugin-1z6` — `make lint` does not cover component specs; I shellchecked the new spec separately, clean.
- No CHANGELOG 4.1 section, no commit — both release decisions, flagged for closeout.

RESOLVED by claude-workflow-plugin-wg6 (C1a), 2026-07-29 — one landing, one migration, as this task's NOTE required.

Three alternatives appended to the single-line `WORKFLOW_DENYLIST_REGEX`:

- `(^|/)\.claude/plans/` — the plan-mode shape (5 of the 6 recorded instances; the one that hard-blocked a task-less session across 3 Stop iterations to J21).

Those two specs would then keep passing while proving nothing. The agreed fix for that class is prompt guidance, now mirrored into `qa.md` §3a and the three specialist prompts.

Both limits are pinned positively, not merely left uncovered: `denylist-lib: agent-chosen /tmp scratch stays reviewable (limit is deliberate)` at L1, and `denylist-D4` at L2 — which pins the limit using the component fixture's OWN `mktemp -d` path, so the assertion fails the moment someone broadens `/tmp` without revisiting the recorded reason.

title: Bug: review-check gate suppressed by embedded newline in a REVIEW-ARTIFACT header field
description:
Discovered during QA of 1vq.1. LATENT (no live release path in V2: the gate predicate is not yet wired to any release credential; the change-set-hash-bound qa-approved record remains the only release path). Track for V3 before review-check.sh gate is wired into enforcement.

QA demonstrated end-to-end: a REVIEW-ARTIFACT whose reviewed_hash string value contains an embedded newline, plus a real critical finding, is (1) accepted by review-check.sh validate-artifact exit 0 (spec-faithful: the specified error-key list is closed with no control-char check); (2) embedded verbatim by qa-gate.sh review-record into the single-line comment grammar; (3) truncated by the gate, which reads only the first line of each comment (jq split on newline, index 0). The risk_threshold and findings tokens fall onto line 2 and are dropped, so the gate reports open_findings=0 and exits 0 (PASS) despite a real blocking finding. Line 1 still begins with the REVIEW-ARTIFACT v1 prefix so it is matched as the findings-less artifact.

Root cause: gate correctness rests on the documented single-line-record invariant, but the record writer (the only writer of the grammar) does not enforce it and validate-artifact does not reject control chars in the scalar header fields (reviewer_identity, reviewer_model, reviewed_hash, iteration).

Mitigation (why medium/latent, not high/live): the attacker-influenced finding text (location/evidence/description) is correctly kept OUT of the comment; only the grammar-checked finding id (^R[0-9]+-F[0-9]+$) and enum severity reach the record. Exploit needs control of a header field, which in the sol-codex path comes from the advisory, independence-gated model and in the qa-claude path from QA itself.

Suggested fix: validate-artifact rejects control chars (newline/CR/tab) in scalar string fields; and/or the gate treats a matched REVIEW-ARTIFACT line that lacks a findings= token as malformed rather than as zero-findings.
close_reason: Fixed in-loop under 1vq.1: review-check.sh validate-artifact rejects control chars in the 10 grammar-embedded scalars (scalar_contains_control_char), and gate treats a REVIEW-ARTIFACT line without a closed findings=[...] bracket as review_artifact_malformed (not zero-findings). L1 + META coverage; exploit closed end-to-end.

## RED evidence (reproduced before fix) — llh.19

Gate-entered. Reproduced all three sub-findings by driving the hooks with crafted PreToolUse/PostToolUse payloads.

**Finding 1 — orchestrator Bash-write bypasses the role guard.**
- `settings.json` PreToolUse matcher is `^(Write|Edit|MultiEdit)$`. `Bash` is NOT in the matcher, so an orchestrator `bash -c 'cat > src/x.ts <<EOF…'` never reaches `prevent-orchestrator-edits.sh`.

**Finding 2 — post-edit.sh does not track Bash-writes.**
- `post-edit.sh` extracts `.tool_input.file_path // .tool_input.path`. A Bash command payload has neither, so it emits `{}` and `changed-files.txt` stays absent. The orchestrator's (or any) Bash-write is invisible to the QA change-set.

**Finding 3 — prevent-orchestrator-edits.sh fails OPEN on ambiguous identity.**
- Write tool with NO identity field present → `{}` (ALLOW).
- Write tool with orchestrator identity in an unprobed field (`.meta.agent_role`) → `{}` (ALLOW).
- The 7-field probe + exact-match-list means any orchestrator identity outside those 7 fields, or absent identity, is permitted to write.

All three are now RED. Fix + boundary doc next.

comments.text:
## FIX applied (NOT approved — left for QA) — llh.19

Owned files only: `prevent-orchestrator-edits.sh`, `post-edit.sh`, `settings.json` + their tests; plus 2 stale lines in `docs/HOOKS.md` that described these scripts. Sibling files (verify-before-stop.sh/invariants.ts; README/WORKFLOW) untouched.

### Fix mechanism
1. **settings.json** — both the PreToolUse (deny) and PostToolUse (track) matchers widened `^(Write|Edit|MultiEdit)$` → `^(Write|Edit|MultiEdit|Bash)$` so Bash now reaches both hooks.
2. **prevent-orchestrator-edits.sh** — added `is_bash_write()` heuristic detecting write-shaped Bash (heredoc-to-file, `>`/`>>` into a path, `tee`, `sed -i`, `perl -i`, `dd of=`, `cp`/`mv`/`install` into the tree), with an explicit transient-sink exemption (`/tmp`, `/dev/null`, `/var/tmp`, `/private/tmp`, fd dups like `2>&1`). Decision logic split into two flags:
   - `IS_WRITE_TOOL` (unambiguous Write/Edit/MultiEdit) and `IS_BASH_WRITE` (heuristic).
   - **Confirmed orchestrator** → deny BOTH (write tool + write-shaped Bash).
   - **Unknown identity + write TOOL** → **fail CLOSED** (deny).
   - **Unknown identity + write-shaped Bash (heuristic only)** → ALLOW (anti-overreach — see boundary below).
   - **Specialist / any known non-orchestrator identity** → allow.
3. **post-edit.sh** — added `extract_bash_write_paths()` (mirrors the same shapes/exemptions) so a Bash-laundered edit's target source path(s) are recovered into `changed-files.txt` and become visible to the QA change-set. Refactored the append loop to track 0..n paths; transient sinks and reads produce no entry.

### Threat-model boundary (honest)
- **Primary guard remains the orchestrator's omitted Write/Edit tools.** This hook is defense-in-depth.
- The Bash-write detector is a **raise-the-bar HEURISTIC, not airtight.** A determined orchestrator can obfuscate (base64→sh, operator built from a var, `python -c`/`node -e` writer). We deliberately do NOT chase those — an arms race in a string parser produces false positives that strangle legitimate Bash.
- **Fail-closed is scoped to the unambiguous Write/Edit TOOLS, NOT the Bash heuristic.** Found by **dogfooding**: this plugin's own live hook fired on my edits because this runtime does not surface `subagent_name` for the top-level agent. Widening the matcher to Bash + fail-closing the heuristic bricked ordinary Bash (any command merely *mentioning* `> file` / `sed -i` / `tee` in a quoted arg, grep pattern, or comment was denied). Resolution: fail-closed only on the definite write tools; an unknown-identity write-shaped Bash is allowed. The residual gap (identity-less orchestrator laundering via Bash) is exactly the "determined orchestrator could obfuscate" boundary already declared out of scope.

### Verification (all green, with the live guard in place)
- `prevent-orchestrator-edits.test.sh`: **31/31** (incl. META-test neutralizing `is_bash_write` → orch-Bash-write DENY flips to ALLOW; the 8 write-shapes; 9 anti-overreach legit-Bash; fail-closed for 3 write tools + unprobed-field; the 2 new heuristic-not-fail-closed cases).
- `post-edit-bash-tracking.test.sh`: **9/9** (Bash heredoc/redirect/sed-i tracked; reads/git/`/tmp`/`/dev/null` NOT tracked; envelope still `{}`).
- Regression: `phase5-synthetic-tests.sh` **33/33** (3.4/3.5/3.6 intact); `agent-mcp-tools-parity` **5/5**; `no-nested-spawn-instructions` **10/10**.
- `make lint` exit 0, 0 findings. `node -e JSON.parse(settings.json)` OK.
- Integrated repro post-fix: holes 1b/3a/3b all DENY; orch git/bd + unknown-id Bash-write + specialist write all ALLOW.

Did NOT run full `make test-all` (siblings mid-edit). No commits. Gate left `entered` (rubric-pending) for QA — NOT approved.

title: mutation-sweep.sh: per-mutant test-cmd inherits parser stdin (mutants.txt), drains it -> sweep stops after ~3-4 mutants
description:
Discovered during G2.6ix re-sweep (claude-workflow-plugin-llh.5).

SYMPTOM: a sweep over targets whose tests read stdin (verify-before-stop.sh / post-edit.sh / qa-gate.sh all do `INPUT=$(cat)`) reports e.g. killed:3 survived:0 generated:56 — only 3-4 of 56 mutants actually run; the rest are silently never processed. The summary looks "clean" (0 survivors) and is dangerously misleading.

ROOT CAUSE: the parser drive loop reads the mutant wire format via `while IFS= read -r line ... done < "$MUTANTS_FILE"` (mutation-sweep.sh ~line 469-502). For each mutant it calls run_mutant, which runs the per-mutant test command in a subshell at ~line 424-427:
    (
        cd "$wt" || exit 1
        CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR="$wt" timeout_cmd "$MUTANT_TEST_TIMEOUT_S" bash -c "$TEST_CMD"
    ) >/dev/null 2>&1 || test_rc=$?
stdin is NOT redirected, so fd0 is inherited from the `while read < mutants.txt` loop. When $TEST_CMD invokes a hook that does `INPUT=$(cat)` (or any bare `cat`/`read`), it consumes the REMAINING lines of mutants.txt. The parser's next `read` then hits EOF and the loop exits — the sweep terminates after only the mutants consumed before the first stdin-reading test.

IMPACT: any sweep whose test-cmd exercises stdin-reading code under-runs catastrophically and reports a falsely-clean survivor set. This silently defeats the whole tier for hook-script targets (the primary use case).

FIX (one line): redirect the per-mutant test invocation's stdin from /dev/null, e.g.
    ) </dev/null >/dev/null 2>&1 || test_rc=$?
on the subshell at ~line 427. (Equivalent: `exec </dev/null` at the top of the subshell, or read the mutants file on a dedicated fd: `while read -u 9 ...; done 9< "$MUTANTS_FILE"`.)

WORKAROUND used in llh.5 (no production edit): prefixed the --test-cmd string with `exec </dev/null;`. With that prefix the sweep correctly processed all 56 mutants.

SECONDARY (lower severity): `MUTANT_TEST_TIMEOUT_S` (and SWEEP_TIMEOUT_S) are read as `${VAR:-default}` AFTER `. "$CONF"` sources mutation.conf, which sets them as plain assignments — so an env-var override is clobbered by the conf value. An operator passing `MUTANT_TEST_TIMEOUT_S=240` on the command line is silently ignored (stays 60). Consider honoring an env override (source conf with `:-` guards, or let a CLI flag win). Workaround: point MUTATION_CONF at a temp conf copy with the desired timeout.

Discovered-from: claude-workflow-plugin-llh.5 (G2.6ix survivor triage). Run that exposed it: .claude/.mutation-runs/20260613T100354Z (killed:3/56) vs the corrected .claude/.mutation-runs/20260613T102846Z (exec </dev/null + 240s timeout, all mutants processed).

comments.text:
<!-- BD-MCP-META: {"kind":"qa-note","source":"qa-agent","from_task":"claude-workflow-plugin-llh.5"} -->
## QA triage (from llh.5 gate review) — ledger impact + severity, NOT fixing here

Confirmed REAL by code read + live repro. Both halves reproduce:
- **stdin-drain** at `mutation-sweep.sh:424-427`: the per-mutant subshell runs `timeout_cmd ... bash -c "$TEST_CMD"` with only `>/dev/null 2>&1` (no stdin redirect); the parser loop reads `< "$MUTANTS_FILE"` (line ~502), so fd0 is the mutants file. All three intended sweep targets read stdin via bare `cat` (`verify-before-stop.sh:478`, `post-edit.sh:19`, `qa-gate.sh:1100` `raw=$(cat)`), so a custom test-cmd exercising them drains the mutants file -> early-stop.
- **conf-clobber** at `mutation-sweep.sh:65-71`: `[ -f "$CONF" ] && . "$CONF"` sources `mutation.conf` (plain assignments `MUTANT_TEST_TIMEOUT_S=60` line 41, `SWEEP_TIMEOUT_S=1800` line 47) BEFORE the `${VAR:-default}` lines, so an env override is silently clobbered.

**Live repro this session:** first re-sweep `20260613T100354Z` = generated 56 / killed 3 / survived 0 (early-stop, falsely-clean). I re-ran a scoped vbs sweep with the `exec </dev/null` workaround + temp-conf timeout and it processed past mutant 6 with 0 survivors — workaround confirmed effective.

### LEDGER IMPACT (for G4 / RELEASE_AUDIT.md) — narrower than first feared

365 does **NOT** retroactively invalidate the v3.4.0 C.3 acceptance numbers. I verified the original C.3 run `20260612T063107Z` processed **all 32 mutants** (killed:4 / survived:28; survivors span `verify-before-stop.sh:175..869` + `post-edit.sh:16..120`) — NOT a 3-4 early-stop. Reason: C.3 used the **default** `--test-cmd` (`DEFAULT_TEST_CMD="bash .claude/scripts/tests/run-tests.sh"`, the L1 suite), whose hook invocations pipe their *own* stdin (`echo '{...}' | bash hook`) and never inherit the sweep's fd0. So the CHANGELOG C.3 claim (32/4/28, 27 genuine/1 equivalent) and the calibration precision 0.9412 (computed over a fixed calibration-set, sweep-independent) both stand.

**But** the bug DOES narrow `RELEASE_AUDIT.md` row **R18** (currently PROVEN): the claim "runs them in throwaway git worktrees against the free L1/L2 tiers" holds only for the **default L1** test-cmd. Any **L2-inclusive custom `--test-cmd`** (which the claim implies is supported, and which is the natural way to exercise hook behavior) silently under-runs via this bug and reports a falsely-clean survivor set. Recommendation for G4: **drop R18 from PROVEN to PROVEN-WITH-CAVEAT** with this row cited, and add to this bug's description an explicit statement that it masks sweep coverage for custom (L2-inclusive) test-cmds. The bug currently documents the symptom but not the R18/C.3 relationship.

### Severity

P2 (current) is arguably light given the bug "silently defeats the whole tier for hook-script targets" with a falsely-clean report — the dangerous part is the *silent* under-run, not a loud failure. Consider P1, OR keep P2 but add a loud guard (assert processed==generated, or fail the sweep if survived==0 AND processed<<generated). Left open and unfixed per llh.5 scope; flagging for the G4 owner.

title: label-milestones invariant structurally cannot pass on approve-flow runs: trace beadsLabelTransitions is a NET diff so transient labels (qa-pending added then removed in-run) are invisible; refine trace capture to record transition EVENTS (e.g. derive from qa-gate.sh tool calls in the stream) or redefine the invariant (qa-approved implies the gate cycle)
notes:
OPEN.

=== FINDING ===

The label-milestones invariant cannot pass on any approve-flow run, structurally — not because the workflow fails the milestone-sequence contract, but because trace.beadsLabelTransitions captures a NET diff (added-minus-removed per task), so labels that are added and then removed within the same run are invisible. qa-pending is the canonical case: every approve-flow adds it (when creating the task) and removes it (when QA approves). Net diff shows neither.

=== EVIDENCE ===

Run-4 trace beadsLabelTransitions (cassettes/seed/node-react-auth-2026-06-12T02-18-12-871Z.jsonl):
  auth-aug   added=[devops]                                  removed=[]
  auth-neb   added=[qa-approved]                             removed=[]
  auth-neb.1 added=[backend, qa-approved]                    removed=[]
  auth-neb.2 added=[frontend, qa-approved]                   removed=[]

Engine verdict (verbatim from evaluateAll on the trace + the run-4-anchored fixture.yaml):
  [FAIL] label-milestones: missing milestone label add(s): [qa-pending] — observed adds across run: [backend, devops, frontend, qa-approved]

But qa-pending WAS demonstrably cycled, multiple times — toolCalls in the same trace include:
  - 'bd --no-daemon label add auth-neb.1 qa-pending'
  - 'bash .../qa-gate.sh enter auth-neb.1' (3+ calls)
  - 'bash .../qa-gate.sh approve auth-neb.1' (which atomically removes qa-pending)
  - identical sequence for auth-neb.2 and auth-neb
  - manual 'bd --no-daemon label remove auth-neb.1 qa-pending' workaround calls (because the qa-gate.sh helper was failing under the bd-daemon recursion bug)

The run cycled the gate correctly across 3 tasks (auth-neb.1, auth-neb.2, auth-neb). Run 3 (cassettes/seed/node-react-auth-2026-06-12T00-50-56-312Z.jsonl) showed the identical failure on a different epic shape (auth-86b lineage). So the invariant has now failed identically across 2 separate live runs on demonstrably correct workflows — that's the structural-cannot-pass evidence.

=== TWO REPAIR OPTIONS ===

Option 1 — refine trace capture to record transition EVENTS (not net diffs):
  - Extend the trace collector to record every label add/remove as an event in a beadsLabelEvents[] field (timestamp, task, op, label).
  - Keep beadsLabelTransitions as-is for backward compatibility.
  - Rewrite the label-milestones invariant to scan beadsLabelEvents for the full milestone sequence (presence of the add events in declared order, regardless of subsequent removes).
  - This is the 'correct' fix: it captures the actual gate-cycle dynamics and lets the invariant assert the contract it's named after.
  - Cost: a small change to the collector + invariant.
  - Derivation source for the events: either intercept the bd CLI's stdout (parse 'Added label X to issue Y' lines), or harvest from the toolCall stream by recognising 'bd ... label add/remove ...' Bash command shapes plus qa-gate.sh approve/block invocations (whose side effects we know).

Option 2 — redefine the invariant: weaken to 'final-state implies cycle' (qa-approved present ⟹ qa-pending was once added):
  - Trivial; doesn't capture intermediate milestones if any are added (currently only qa-pending → qa-approved exists in the fixtures, so this is fine TODAY).
  - Honest about what the trace can observe.
  - Loses signal for any future milestone (e.g. qa-blocked → qa-pending re-entry in a block-then-fix cycle would be invisible).

Recommendation: Option 1. It costs a bounded amount of capture code and unblocks any future milestone-progression invariant (J21 escalation states, block-then-recover handshakes). Option 2 is a tactical workaround that hides the cause.

=== HANDOFF ===

Standalone bug (no parent epic). Carries past Phase B. P2 because:
  - It does not affect production workflows; the gate works correctly.
  - It only affects the in-test invariant evaluator and our ability to assert milestone progression.
  - It cannot be fixed by tightening the workflow; the fix is in the trace capture layer or the invariant definition layer.

Evidence anchored: _phase-b-run4-trace.unit.spec.ts (pin on the verbatim engine failure string, run 4) and _phase-b-run3-trace.unit.spec.ts (same failure on run 3 — confirms 'structurally cannot pass on approve-flow runs', not 'run-4 happens to have a coincidence').

notes:
CLOSED 2026-06-12 — completed-with-followup.

=== SCOPE COMPLETED ===

Cue shipped to 2 surfaces and verified IN-FILE on the live repo:
  - verify-before-stop.sh lines 977-982 — FIRST: for every changed file ... impact_of (code-graph MCP) ... fold high-fan-in callers ... fall back to grep/code_search; do not silently skip.
  - qa.md section 3a, lines 154/158/160 — FIRST ACTION: Before reading the diff, before running review modules, before writing review notes — run impact_of (code-graph MCP) on each changed exported symbol AND on each whole changed file.

Failing-test-first captured: .claude/scripts/tests/qa-impact-of-cue.test.sh — 4 PRE-FIX failures, all flipped to PASS post-fix. Meta-tests in place.

=== POST-FIX LIVE VALIDATION (run 4) ===

Run 4 (cassettes/seed/node-react-auth-2026-06-12T02-18-12-871Z.jsonl, 2026-06-12, ~$5.46, 1376s, 41 turns, success): satisfiesInvariants evaluated LIVE for the first time (366.8's effect; fixture.yaml preserved end-to-end). Engine verdict on the run-4 trace:
  - 3 PASS (stop-requires-approval, orchestrator-no-edits, declared-subagents-only)
  - 1 SKIP (completion-contract — documented trace gap)
  - 2 FAIL (label-milestones — structural NET-diff bug, see new bug claude-workflow-plugin-9ke; qa-queried-impact-of — 0 impact_of calls AGAIN despite cue shipping)

The fix in this task did NOT move QA's impact_of invocation rate. Root cause: the cue is on the right surfaces (qa.md 3a is in every QA spawn's system prompt; verify-before-stop.sh's heredoc has the cue at the repo level) but the cue does not actually reach QA via the channels we assumed:
  - The Stop-hook recovery template fires ONLY on Stop block-then-recover cycles. In a clean-flow run where the orchestrator delegates to QA proactively (no block needed), the heredoc never fires.
  - For RUN 4 specifically, the Stop hook DID fire (2 blocks), BUT the fixture-local script that ran is the stale render (last touched a8a7bcf 'v3 upgrade + G8 test harness' — predates 8f07ea9 366.9 cue fix). Hooks.json resolves to CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/.claude/scripts/verify-before-stop.sh which is the fixture-rendered (stale) copy, not the repo copy. Cue absent from both block reasons (anchored in _phase-b-run4-trace.unit.spec.ts).
  - qa.md 3a IS in every QA spawn's system prompt. 4 live runs (run 1/2/3/4) all show 0 impact_of calls. In-system-prompt prose alone is empirically insufficient.

=== SUPERSEDED BY ===

New standalone bug **claude-workflow-plugin-n6d** (p1) — 'impact_of cue does not reach QA on clean-flow runs ... qa.md 3a alone empirically insufficient (4 live runs, 0 calls)'. Carries the cue-channel problem forward past Phase B with the mechanical option (orchestrator pre-computes impact_of and embeds results in the QA delegation packet) added to the design menu inherited from this task.

Closing as completed-with-followup: the cue ships, the failing-test-first L1 captures it, the gap is now in a separate bug with explicit run-4 citations. Phase B's QA mandate (cue present in code) is satisfied; QA mandate (cue effective) is in the follow-up bug.

Live run-4 demonstrated the cue is in the wrong delivery channels (fixture-stale Stop-hook copy lacked the cue; qa.md 3a alone empirically insufficient over 4 live runs). Superseded by new standalone bug claude-workflow-plugin-n6d with run-4 evidence + the mechanical 'orchestrator pre-computes impact_of' design option.

comments.author: username
comments.text:
<!-- BD-MCP-META: {"kind":"repro-evidence","source":"qa-agent","observed_on":"claude-workflow-plugin-gl6","bd_version":"0.47.1"} -->
## REPRODUCED — the removal is not a no-op; it is silently REVERTED by a stale-JSONL auto-import (WAL mtime blind spot)

Observed 2026-07-28 on `claude-workflow-plugin-gl6` during a QA gate cycle, bd v0.47.1.
This converts the suspected "silent no-op" into a named, reproducible divergence. Per
the 0.5 evidence-before-fix protocol: **no patch proposed here** — this is the
reproduction + root-cause statement only.

### The symptom that started it
Across two QA rounds, both QA and the implementer independently believed they had
cleared `qa-blocked` on gl6, and the label was present anyway at the next spawn.
QA's round-2 `bd_update_task(remove_labels=["qa-blocked"])` returned a label set
that did NOT contain `qa-blocked`; one round later `bd show` listed it again.

### What I actually observed (not inferred)
1. `bd label remove claude-workflow-plugin-gl6 qa-blocked` — **succeeds**:
   `✓ Removed label 'qa-blocked' from claude-workflow-plugin-gl6`, `rc=0`.
   So the remove path itself is NOT broken and stderr is not hiding a failure.
2. Immediately after, the two stores **disagree**:
   - `bd show` / `sqlite3 .beads/beads.db "select … from labels …"` ->
     `devops,qa-gate-entered,qa-pending,rubric-pending` (removal applied)
   - `.beads/issues.jsonl` -> `["devops","qa-blocked","qa-gate-entered","qa-pending","rubric-pending"]`
     with `updated_at` frozen at an earlier write (`2026-07-28T01:18:20`)
3. `bd label remove` does **not** bump `updated_at` and does **not** flush the JSONL.
4. A subsequent `bd update --notes …` (rc=0) also did **not** flush: DB advanced to
   `01:40:01` / 4 labels, JSONL stayed at `01:18:20` / 5 labels including `qa-blocked`.
5. The sync daemon is live (`✓ running (PID 32578, v0.47.1)`, mode `events`,
   interval 5s) and had still not flushed ~5 minutes of DB writes.
6. **The file mtimes are the tell.** SQLite is in `wal` journal mode:
   ```
   2026-07-28 01:35:16   .beads/beads.db        <- stale
   2026-07-28 01:40:01   .beads/beads.db-wal    <- where my writes actually landed
   2026-07-28 01:35:16   .beads/issues.jsonl    <- equal to beads.db, older than the real state
   ```
7. bd's own help documents both halves of the mechanism:
   `--no-auto-flush  Disable automatic JSONL sync after CRUD operations`
   `--no-auto-import Disable automatic JSONL import when newer than DB`

### Root-cause statement
**A label removal lands in the SQLite WAL and is not flushed to `issues.jsonl`;
because `beads.db`'s mtime does not advance while writes sit in `beads.db-wal`, any
later touch of the git-tracked `issues.jsonl` makes it look NEWER than the DB, so
bd's auto-import replays the pre-removal label set over the newer DB state — and the
removal appears to have silently no-op'd.**

Evidence: items 1-7 above; the divergence in item 2 is directly observed, and
`issues.jsonl` is a tracked file that routinely shows as modified in `git status` in
this repo, so the "JSONL touched after the DB" precondition is met constantly.

### Honest scoping — what is inference, not observation
I did **not** instrument bd to confirm the import comparison reads `beads.db`'s mtime
rather than `max(beads.db, beads.db-wal)`. That specific step is inferred from the
help text plus the observed 5-minute staleness. The *divergence* and the *stale JSONL
containing the removed label* are directly observed and are enough to reproduce.
A deterministic test should assert on the divergence, not on my inferred comparison.

### Why the gate contract survived this
`qa-approved` is set by the same code path, so the release credential was never
falsely granted — matching the earlier note that "qa-approved was set correctly so the
Stop-hook contract held". The failure mode is a **stale blocking label persisting**,
i.e. fail-closed noise, not a fail-open release. That is why this has stayed cosmetic
so far, and also why it is easy to keep mis-attributing to agents forgetting to clear it.

### Suggested reproduction skeleton (for whoever writes the failing test)
1. `bd label add <tid> qa-blocked`; wait for a JSONL flush; confirm both stores agree.
2. `bd label remove <tid> qa-blocked`; confirm DB says removed and JSONL still says present.
3. `touch .beads/issues.jsonl` (simulating any git/tool write), then run any `bd` read.
4. Assert the label is still absent. Today the expectation is that it comes back.

Cross-ref: observed during the gl6 v4.1 U1 gate cycle; the 36z precedent in the same
wave shows QA clearing `qa-blocked` explicitly alongside `approve`, which is the
current workaround.

title: docs/specs/<tid>.md has no durability-across-approve spec, unlike its sibling docs/reviews/
description:
From QA round 4 of D2 (R4-F1, low), 2026-08-17.

rqer built review-artifact-durability.sh specifically to prove that docs/reviews/<tid>-r<n>.json SURVIVES a
completed approve — the property that whole task existed to establish, pinned by a dedicated spec with its
own mutation pairing.

D2 introduced a sibling tracked-path class, docs/specs/<tid>.md, and gave it no equivalent. The property
IS load-bearing — upgrade-gate-compat's legs 4b and 7-META depend on the file surviving and being bound —
but it is pinned only INDIRECTLY, as a side effect of assertions about other things.

That asymmetry is exactly how the three acceptance failures happened: docs/reviews/ was taught to the
machinery and docs/specs/ was not, and nothing tested the second directly enough to notice.

NEEDS: a durability spec for docs/specs/<tid>.md in the shape of review-artifact-durability.sh — four-part
pairing, with the mutation being whatever would delete or fail to bind it, and a leg driving a real
completed approve.

title: qa-gate.sh exit 3 is overloaded: the contract table documents one meaning, j7kk added another
description:
From the D2 SCOPE RE-AUDIT, confirmed still live after D2 Part B (which deliberately did not touch exit 3).

  qa-gate.sh:133-145  the exit-code contract table documents 3 as 'atomic operation rolled back'
  qa-gate.sh:2807-2817  j7kk's STATUS-UNAVAILABLE region emits exit 3 for 'the store could not be read'

The per-subcommand help at :20-24 documents the new meaning; the contract table does not. Two distinct
conditions, one code, one of them undocumented where a caller would look.

Both are correctly fail-closed, so this is a documentation-and-contract defect rather than a live hole. It
matters because the contract table is what a future author reads when choosing a code for a NEW refusal —
D2 just chose exit 2 for its design refusal partly by reading that table, and got it right for reasons the
table does not fully capture.

NEEDS: either give the store-unavailable condition its own code, or amend the table to document both
meanings and say how a caller distinguishes them. Note the re-audit measured 5, 6 and 7 as literally
unused in qa-gate.sh and review-check.sh, so a new code is available.

title: review-record --file: validated bytes and hashed bytes can diverge when CWD != PROJECT_DIR (repo-relative spelling)
description: QA round-1 finding R1-F5 on claude-workflow-plugin-rqer (deferred there as a follow-up, filed now in round 2). cmd_review_record with --file in the repo-relative spelling reads the artifact via cat -- <relative> (CWD-relative, qa-gate.sh:4933) for validation and grammar extraction, but hashes the absolute derived path. With CWD != PROJECT_DIR and different files at both spellings, the validated/extracted bytes and the hashed bytes diverge: the record's verdict fields can describe different bytes than artifact_hash names. Self-inflicted-only edge (no privilege boundary). FIX SHAPE per the round-1 artifact: resolve input_path against PROJECT_DIR before reading, or read raw from the derived path after the derivation check. Evidence: docs/reviews/claude-workflow-plugin-rqer-r1.json finding R1-F5.

title: upgrade-gate-compat META 7 was deliberately weakened from equality to shape during rqer — tighten it back
description:
From QA round 1 of rqer, 2026-08-15. Recorded by QA as structurally justified AND worth tightening, so
it is filed rather than left in a commit message.

During rqer, .claude/tests/component/specs/upgrade-gate-compat.sh's META 7 was changed from an EQUALITY
assertion to a SHAPE assertion, because the artifact_hash= token made the previous byte-exact expectation
untenable. QA ruled the weakening structurally justified for that round and explicitly flagged it as a
precision loss to recover.

WHY IT MATTERS: a META-TEST is the negative control that proves its own guard is load-bearing. A shape
assertion admits a class of mutants an equality assertion would have caught, so the control is weaker
than the day before, and nothing else records that.

NEEDS: restore an equality-strength assertion that accommodates the new token — for example pinning the
full expected record with artifact_hash= interpolated, rather than matching a looser pattern.

DISCOVERED-FROM: rqer QA round 1.

title: review-record --file in repo-relative spelling from a foreign CWD can validate one file and hash another
description:
From QA round 1 of rqer (R1-F5, LOW), 2026-08-15.

review-record's --file arm resolves the supplied path against the CALLER's working directory, while the
derivation and hashing steps resolve against the project root. Invoked with a repo-relative spelling
from a CWD that is not the project root, the validation can read one file and the hash can be taken over
another.

Bounded today: the derived-path refusal (artifact_path_not_derived) closes the common shapes, and QA
found no live case. It is filed because the two-resolution-contexts pattern is the same shape as the
governing-veto path-resolution defect (mdnc), which took a full round to close and was ALSO measured
rather than reasoned about.

FIX SHAPE: resolve --file against the project root exactly once, before both validation and hashing, and
refuse if the two ever disagree. The in-repo precedent is design_artifact_path_for()'s single
derivation.

title: impact-report.sh accepts a flag as a task id, writing impact-report---change-set-hash.json
description:
Pre-existing, surfaced by QA during Batch B round 1, 2026-08-14. NOT this batch's work.

.claude/.qa-tracking/ contains 'impact-report---change-set-hash.json' and 'impact-report---list.json'.
Both are the product of invoking impact-report.sh with a FLAG where a task id was expected: the script
took '--change-set-hash' as a positional task id and wrote a report named after it.

Consequence: junk artifacts accumulate with names that look like real per-task reports, and a caller who
mistypes gets a written file plus a success exit rather than a usage error. The approve-time freshness
refusal keys on the per-task report path, so a plausibly-named junk file in that directory is worse than
an absent one.

model to copy - reject, never sanitise.
